output.summary: The conflict-round change is mostly sound: the trigger, durable pending rows, one-in-flight and daily-cap checks, the pinned push with lease, and the land-entry relabel all work as specified. The new test file passes 21/21 in a clean copy, typecheck is clean, and biome reports only a pre-existing warning. Two defects need fixing before merge: the review-rejection test never produces a valid review verdict (invalid fixture, so it passes for the wrong reason), and allowEmpty disables the empty-diff audit for every resolution, so a resolution that drops the PR's change is pushed (reproduced). Smaller issues: a dead "already resolved" guard, silent trigger skips, a non-additive migration, auto-merge disabled before validation, and some test-coverage gaps. Nine failures in gates, github-notifier and providers-cli reproduce at base, so they predate the change. land-pr.test.ts passes 115/115 alone at head; its failure in the full run is cross-test leakage. The full suite did not finish in this session.

findings.title: The review-rejection case never reaches a valid review verdict
findings.detail: The fake review returns verdict "changes", but ReviewSchema accepts only approve | request_changes. The finding also omits security, suggestion, failure_scenario, category, confidence and introduced_by_diff, so every model fails structured-output validation. The run ends needs_human with "No model available for review ... structured output failed validation". The test "a resolution rejected by %s does not push" (review case) therefore passes without any request_changes verdict being processed. Reproduced by running the original fixture: outcome needs_human, error "No model available for review after: alpha/m: structured output failed validation". With a schema-valid request_changes fixture the run also ends needs_human with no push, so the behaviour is right, but this test does not show it.
findings.suggestion: Use verdict "request_changes" and a complete finding object. Assert that the review stage recorded request_changes, so a fixture error cannot satisfy the case.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression where a valid request_changes verdict is mishandled and the round pushes anyway would still pass this test, because the test never produces a valid rejection.

findings.title: allowEmpty disables the empty-diff audit for every resolution, so a resolution that drops the PR's change is pushed
findings.detail: auditDiff now skips the empty-diff block whenever resolution is true (engine.ts:1223, audit.ts:204). The audited diff is measured against the base tip (run.baseSha), so an empty diff means the resolved tree equals the base tree. That happens either because the PR's change was already in base, or because the implementer discarded the PR's change. The audit cannot tell these apart and now passes both. Reproduced in a temp copy: an implementer that writes base's version of greeting.txt gives "audit succeeded +0/-0 in 0 files; 0 blocking", the review approves, and delivery pushes a merge commit whose greeting.txt is "base intent". The PR's "PR intent" change is silently gone. Before this change the same run stopped at empty-diff. The exemption was meant for the clean-merge case, where the implementer does not run (covered by the test "a clean merge with the base's exact tree").
findings.suggestion: Limit the exemption to rounds where the factory made the merge without implementer edits, for example allowEmpty only when the implementer did not run for this round. Add a test that a resolution taking the base's content ends needs_human with no push.
findings.failure_scenario: The implementer resolves the conflict by taking the base's version of a PR-changed file. The diff against base is empty, audit passes, review approves on the strength of the LLM alone, and the PR branch receives a merge commit that drops the PR's change.

findings.title: The "head already resolved" guard checks the wrong field and is effectively unreachable
findings.detail: The check requires a conflict row with reviewedSha === trigger.head and deliveredSha set. After a real delivery the PR head is deliveredSha, so a trigger for the current head does not match a row whose reviewedSha equals it. Stale triggers already fail with "PR head moved". The test that expects "already resolved" passes only because it never advances the fake remote head, so it asserts a state that cannot occur after a real delivery.
findings.suggestion: Remove the check, or compare deliveredSha with trigger.head and test with the advanced remote head. A CONFLICTING report for a delivered head means base moved again and should start a round.
findings.failure_scenario: A round delivers head Y. Later the poller reports Y as CONFLICTING. The guard does not suppress it, and the test suggests it should. The test gives false confidence about the daily-cap and resolved-head behaviour.

findings.title: Skipped conflict triggers are final and the conflict stalls silently
findings.detail: A trigger that hits a transient reason ("round in flight", "conflict round daily cap reached", "PR head moved") is marked skipped and never revisited. The poller emits pr.conflicting only on a transition into CONFLICTING, and land entries are not re-blocked, so a PR that is still CONFLICTING when the blocking round ends gets no conflict round and no feed item until another event happens. The spec's "starts none" for a second trigger supports dropping it, but the stall is invisible.
findings.suggestion: Write a feed item for each skipped conflict trigger that includes its reason, or re-evaluate pending conflict observations for a PR when a round on it finishes.
findings.failure_scenario: A human review round is in flight when the poller reports the PR CONFLICTING. The trigger is skipped. The review round delivers. The PR stays CONFLICTING, and nothing starts or reports a conflict round.

findings.title: Migration rebuilds review_rounds, which contradicts the additive-migration rule
findings.detail: AGENTS.md and the migrations README require additive migrations so the previous release can keep running. This file drops and rebuilds review_rounds and both feed triggers, and changes uniqueness from (pr_url, round) to (pr_url, kind, round). After a rollback, the previous release will count conflict rows toward the review cap (createReviewRound uses rounds.length), list them as review rounds, and treat an in-flight conflict run as a review round. The data is preserved, so this is not corruption.
findings.suggestion: If the rebuild is unavoidable, state the rollback behaviour in the migration header and in the release notes. Otherwise keep the old constraint and number conflict rounds in a separate column or table.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is rolled back after a conflict round exists. The old release counts that row toward the review round cap and treats the conflict run as a review round.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before the grant and head are validated
findings.detail: In deliverReviewRound, gh pr merge --disable-auto runs right after readPrHead and before remoteBranchSha, stored() and assertFactoryBranchPush. If the PR head has moved or the grant changed, the delivery is refused, but auto-merge has already been turned off. Disabling must happen before the push, so only the ordering is wrong.
findings.suggestion: Move the disable after the grant and head checks and immediately before pushExistingBranch.
findings.failure_scenario: A human pushes to the PR during delivery. The round is refused, yet the PR's auto-merge has been disabled as a side effect.

findings.title: The snapshot path re-implements prHeadProblem and skips the branch check when headRefName is absent
findings.detail: startConflictTrigger's snapshot branch repeats the PR checks inline instead of reusing prHeadProblem, and the branch check runs only when seen.headRefName is truthy. Snapshots saved before this change lack headRefName, so the check passes. Delivery re-checks through prHeadProblem and fails closed, but the trigger has already started a round, which counts toward the daily cap. This goes against AGENTS.md's one-guard rule.
findings.suggestion: Build a PrHead from the snapshot (state, headRefName, isCrossRepository, headRepository, headRefOid) and call prHeadProblem, treating missing fields as a refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: An old snapshot without headRefName is used for a PR whose head branch has since changed. A round starts and uses up cap, then delivery refuses it.

findings.title: Conflict rounds force the quick profile, which narrows review regardless of the owner's profile
findings.detail: Every conflict round sets resolvedProfile to quick. That gives a single standard review, no holdout and no acceptance check, even for an owner run that was deep. The spec asks for gates, audit and review of the resolution and does not mention a profile change, so the downgrade is an unstated decision.
findings.suggestion: Either inherit the owner's profile, or document the choice in the change description and say why a rewritten merge needs less review.
findings.failure_scenario: A deep owner PR with a non-trivial conflict resolution is reviewed by one standard reviewer and gets no holdout, so the resolution gets less scrutiny than the original work.

findings.title: The land-entry relabel only matches reasons that start with 'conflicts with'
findings.detail: markRoundDelivered updates the land reason only where it still reads "conflicts with %". A poller-triggered round can deliver while the entry is queued at the old approved head. The entry then blocks as "head moved after approval", the update does not match, and the reason never names the new head. The feed item does name it. Spec item 3 covers a land entry blocked by the conflict, so this path is not fully covered.
findings.suggestion: Also relabel a blocked entry whose approvedSha is the reviewed head of the delivered round, or give the land queue a conflict reason on that path.
findings.failure_scenario: A poller-triggered resolution is delivered while the land entry is queued at the old head. The entry ends blocked with "head moved after approval" and does not mention the new head.

findings.title: The non-factory poller case bypasses the poller
findings.detail: The test named "polling records and consumes the non-factory conflict observation" never starts the poller for that case. It inserts a trigger by hand and calls startConflictTrigger directly. The spec's non-factory requirement is about what the poller emits, so the poller's handling of untracked or non-factory PRs is not tested.
findings.suggestion: Drive the non-factory case through startGitHubPoller with a PR that has no factory owner, or rename the test so it does not claim poller coverage.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller starts a round for a non-factory PR because nothing in the poller path filters it, and no test notices.

findings.title: The heartbeat test asserts nothing about heartbeats
findings.detail: "a blocked entry stops heartbeating while its conflict trigger verifies the PR" never checks heartbeat behaviour. It asserts only that one round exists after queue.stop().
findings.suggestion: Rename it to describe what it checks, or assert the heartbeat behaviour it names.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression in heartbeat handling during conflict verification would not be caught by this test.

output.summary: Reviewed the conflict-round change against the M5.5 request: the land-queue and pr.conflicting triggers, durable pending rows, per-PR in-flight and daily-cap checks, the conflict run kind, pinned-refspec delivery, the gate/audit/review failure paths, and the land blocked-reason update. The 21 new tests in test/conflict-rounds.test.ts pass in a temp copy of HEAD (dependencies installed there; the worktree has no node_modules), and `tsc --noEmit` passes. Biome reports one warning in an unchanged file. The existing suites I ran pass: github-poller 60/60, migrations 21/21, review-round 3/3, land-queue 41/41, feed-store 9/9, pipeline-review-restart 3/3, pipeline-conflicts 16/16, and review-rounds 24/25 with the single failure a 30s timeout that passes alone. The timeouts came from my concurrent load, not the change. Not run: the full `bun test` and the other pipeline-* suites. The main defect is that a land requested by PR URL or number after any conflict round resolves to the round run, whose baseBranch is the PR head branch, so the land never merges or checks the current base. The remaining findings are minor. The non-test source added is roughly 380 lines, within budget.

findings.title: Land by PR URL or number resolves to the conflict-round run and uses the PR head branch as base
findings.detail: LandQueue.request resolves its target with getRun(target) ?? runForPr(prRef(target)). runForPr (src/db/store.ts:2489) returns the newest run with that pr_url, which after this change is the conflict-round run. That run is created with baseBranch = owner.branch (the PR head branch), so the land entry gets baseBranch = limitless/owner-feature instead of main. fetchBase, checks and mergeBase then use the feature branch as the base, so the merge with the current base and its checks never run. The docs (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:317) promise that the land merges in the base when it has moved and runs checks from that base. Review rounds already carry the same baseBranch and pr_url, so the root cause predates this change. The conflict flow makes it the default: after a round, 'approve the new head to land' with `limitless land <pr>` picks the round run. I confirmed this with a probe test in the temp copy: after a conflict round exists, request({target: <PR URL>}) returned runId = the round run and baseBranch = 'limitless/owner-feature'.
findings.suggestion: In LandQueue.request, resolve the owner before reading base or branch: `const owner = this.store.reviewRound(run.id)?.owner ?? run`, then use owner.id, owner.baseBranch, and owner.deliveryBranch ?? owner.branch. Alternatively, make runForPr skip runs whose sourceRef.kind is 'review-round'. Add a test that requests a land by PR URL after a conflict round and asserts baseBranch is main and the entry's runId is the owner's.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict round for PR #1 (base feature branch limitless/owner-feature) has been delivered. The user runs `limitless land https://github.com/test/repo/pull/1`. runForPr returns the round run, so the entry gets baseBranch = limitless/owner-feature. main has since gained commits. The land is 'checked' against the feature branch: the head is already a descendant of it, so no merge with main happens, and the land checks run on a head that was never merged with current main. If CI passes on that head, the squash-merge goes through with main's new commits unchecked.

findings.title: allowEmpty lets a resolution that drops the whole PR change pass the empty-diff audit
findings.detail: For resolution rounds, engine.ts:1223 passes allowEmpty: resolution, so the empty-diff rule is skipped. oneRound measures the audit diff against ctx.run.baseSha, which mergeForDelivery sets to the base tip. If the implementer resolves every conflict by taking the base's side, the merged tree equals base, the diff is empty, and audit passes. Review is then the only check that the PR's intent survived. The test 'a clean merge with the base's exact tree' covers only the case where the PR's change is already contained in base. It does not distinguish that from a resolution that discards the PR's change.
findings.suggestion: Allow an empty diff only when the pre-merge PR head's own change against the base is already empty (the PR change was contained in base before the merge). Otherwise keep the empty-diff block for resolution rounds, or record the dropped PR change as a finding.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR adds greeting.txt 'PR intent'. The base also changed greeting.txt. The implementer takes the base's version of every conflicted hunk and no other file changes. The diff against base is empty, allowEmpty bypasses the audit, and only the reviewer judges whether the PR's intent was lost.

findings.title: Migration rebuilds review_rounds and is not additive, against the migration README
findings.detail: src/db/migrations/README.md says schema changes must be additive so the previous release can open the database after a rollback. This migration drops the review_rounds table and both of its feed triggers and recreates them. It also changes the uniqueness to (pr_url, kind, round). The old release can still open the database, because its inserts omit kind and default to 'review'. But after a rollback, the old code's reviewRounds() and reviewRound() return conflict rows as review rounds. Those rows count toward the old release's review cap and its in-flight check. If a conflict run is still queued at rollback, the old release would run it as a review round.
findings.suggestion: Store conflict rounds in a new table keyed by run id, or add a nullable column without rebuilding review_rounds. If the rebuild has to stay, document the rollback caveat next to the migration and add a rollback test.
findings.failure_scenario: After a rollback to the previous release, a conflict round row (kind='conflict') exists for PR #1. The old reviewRounds() counts it toward the 3-round cap and reports it as in flight, so a human's changes-requested verdict is refused as 'still in flight' until the round terminates.

findings.title: Conflict rounds force the quick profile instead of the owner's, so the resolution review uses the quick roster
findings.detail: Review rounds run with profile: owner.profile (src/pipeline/review-round.ts:200). Conflict rounds are inserted with profile 'quick' (store.ts:1150) and prepare pins resolvedProfile 'quick' (engine.ts:541). profile() then selects the quick review roster in panel mode and skips the AC verify stage and holdout. The request says the resolution goes through gates, audit and review, and says to reuse the review-round machinery, which uses the owner's profile. The quick choice is deliberate in the code but not stated in the request.
findings.suggestion: Use owner.profile for the review and gate selection, and skip only the spec stage (for example with an explicit flag), or record the quick choice in the PR comment and in the request notes.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR built under the 'deep' profile in panel mode gets its conflict resolution reviewed by the quick roster. The resolution can ship with a weaker review than the original change had.

findings.title: Conflict delivery disables the PR's auto-merge before the lock-held checks and before any push
findings.detail: deliverReviewRound runs `gh pr merge --disable-auto` for conflict rounds before stored() and assertFactoryBranchPush, and before the push. If either check then refuses the delivery, the PR's auto-merge is still disabled and nothing was pushed. Disabling is the safe direction, and review-round.ts:198 does the same for changes-requested verdicts. The side effect is not in the request and is not mentioned in the PR comment.
findings.suggestion: Move the disable to just before the push, after the refusal checks, or mention in the PR comment that auto-merge was disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR's head moves during the round. The delivery refuses with 'head moved', but the PR's auto-merge was turned off by the attempt and stays off until someone re-enables it.

findings.title: Skipped triggers are permanent and silent, leaving the land entry blocked with no explanation
findings.detail: startConflictTrigger marks a trigger 'skipped' with a reason (round in flight, daily cap reached, PR head moved, not open, and so on). Nothing else is written: no feed item, no land event, no retry. For a land entry the reason stays 'conflicts with main' and nothing says that the conflict is not being resolved. The request asks only that starting exactly one round is enforced. It does not forbid recording the skip, but a silent dead end is hard to diagnose.
findings.suggestion: Write a land or feed event with the skip reason when a land-sourced trigger is skipped, so the operator can see why no round started.
findings.failure_scenario: A changes-requested review round is in flight when the land is blocked. The land trigger is skipped with 'round in flight'. The round delivers, and the entry stays 'conflicts with main' with no record that a conflict resolution was ever attempted.

findings.title: Startup and land-path triggers trust a stored PR snapshot that may be stale
findings.detail: processConflictTriggers reads the stored PR snapshot and skips the live lookup whenever one exists. startConflictTrigger's draft, fork, branch and open checks then use that snapshot. If the PR was closed, converted to draft, or re-pointed since the last poll, a round still starts. It runs gates and model calls before delivery's readPrHead refuses it. Delivery does recheck, so nothing is pushed, but the work and the daily-cap slot are spent.
findings.suggestion: For land-sourced and startup triggers, consult the live PR state (readPrHead) before starting a round, or keep the snapshot path only for poller-sourced triggers whose observation is fresh.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last saw PR #1 open and mergeable. The PR was then converted to draft and a land is blocked with a conflict. The trigger starts a conflict round on the stored snapshot. The round runs its full pipeline, then delivery throws 'the PR is draft', and the run fails after the model calls.

findings.title: Test gaps: PR-URL land after a round, disable-auto, and audit on the clean-merge case
findings.detail: The suite never requests a land by PR URL or number after a conflict round, which is how the baseBranch defect above slipped through. It does not assert that `gh pr merge --disable-auto` ran during a conflict delivery; the fake gh only clears a flag. The 'clean merge with the base's exact tree' test asserts a review stage but never checks that audit ran or passed on that run.
findings.suggestion: Add a land-by-URL test that expects baseBranch = main and a runId equal to the owner. Assert the disable-auto call and the audit stage explicitly.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that changes the land target lookup, or drops the disable-auto call, passes the full new suite unnoticed.

output.summary: Reviewed the change against issue #487 by reading the diff, generating the real gate and editor Seatbelt profile text through homeReadPolicy/seatbeltProfile, and running the targeted suites from a TMPDIR copy of HEAD with an empty HOME. The core design is sound: gates deny the home subpath and re-allow the checkout, scratch, recorded Git paths and toolchains; editors deny the ten listed credential stores through one module; overlaps and unresolved homes fail closed before anything runs. Two major gaps remain. The gate allowlist grants the whole CARGO_HOME, which holds the crates.io token, so a gate can read it. A factory data directory outside $HOME (LIMITLESS_HOME, documented) is never denied, so other runs' checkouts stay readable from gates. Real-Seatbelt probes could not run here (nested sandbox-exec refused, 9 tests skipped), so the Seatbelt-dependent claims rest on profile text and last-match semantics, not on a live run. Test results on HEAD with empty HOME: sandbox 15 pass/9 skip, gates 92 pass/2 skip, harness 56 pass, signal and confinement suites pass, scratch 88 pass/4 skip/2 fail; both scratch failures also fail on the base commit (no temp dir writable in this sandbox). Biome lint was not run (not installed in the worktree).

findings.title: Gates can read the cargo registry token under CARGO_HOME
findings.detail: homeReadPolicy adds the whole CARGO_HOME (default ~/.cargo) to allowRead for gates. The gate profile emits (deny file-read* (subpath <home>)) and then (allow file-read* (subpath <home>/.cargo)), and Seatbelt is last-match-wins, so ~/.cargo/credentials.toml (and any registry tokens in ~/.cargo/config.toml) becomes readable. The credentials list (ssh, gh, aws, ...) does not include cargo, and no specific deny is generated because specificDenies only covers denyRead entries under an allow. I confirmed this from the generated profile: '(allow file-read* ... (subpath ".../home/.cargo") ...)' with no rule covering credentials.toml. The issue requires every credential store to fall outside the gate allowlist, and the spec names only the cargo home as a toolchain, which the implementation widened to the full credential-bearing home.
findings.suggestion: Allow only the toolchain binaries the gate needs (for rustup proxies, CARGO_HOME/bin) instead of the whole CARGO_HOME. runConfined already copies config.toml from the trusted side before candidate code runs, so the gate does not need the directory itself. Add a gate probe: head -c 1 on $HOME/.cargo/credentials.toml must be denied while cargo --version still works. Update docs/GUIDE.md and ARCHITECTURE.md, which currently say the cargo home is readable.
findings.failure_scenario: A user has run `cargo login`, so ~/.cargo/credentials.toml holds a crates.io token. A candidate's Rust gate command (or a build.rs or test in a Dependabot PR) runs `cat ~/.cargo/credentials.toml`. The allow subpath for ~/.cargo matches after the home deny, so the token is read and printed into gate output or sent out over HTTPS.

findings.title: Factory data directory outside $HOME is not denied to gates or editors
findings.detail: The home-wide gate deny covers only $HOME. The factory data directory is LIMITLESS_HOME (config.ts:143) or overrides.home, which docs/GUIDE.md:900 and :992 document as movable. configureReadPolicy receives only the config dir (config.ts:315), so paths.home, and with it paths.runs, paths.work and paths.repos, is never denied. I evaluated homeReadPolicy with a stand-in home and a stand-in other-run checkout under a data dir outside it: the gate denyRead did not cover it (case C). Its checkout and any other run's files there are readable from a gate, and the spec requires other runs' checkouts and the data directory to fall outside the allowlist. The DB is still protected through privateReadPaths, so only the checkouts and other per-run files are exposed.
findings.suggestion: Pass the data directory into the read policy (for example configureReadPolicy(raw.sandbox, configDir, paths.home)) and add it to the deny list for gates, the same way home is denied. The run's own checkout, repos cache and scratch stay allowed by the existing allow rules. Add a test with home and LIMITLESS_HOME outside it, asserting that another run's checkout is denied and the current checkout is readable.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets LIMITLESS_HOME=/Volumes/data/limitless. Candidate code in one run's gate runs `cat /Volumes/data/limitless/runs/<other-run>/worktree/.env`, which is allowed because nothing in the profile denies that subtree. Other runs' unlanded code, and any secrets in their worktrees, are exposed.

findings.title: Other invocations' scratch in the shared temp directory stays readable from gates
findings.detail: Gates allow reads of the whole $TMPDIR tree (only home, credentials and DB are denied), so other invocations' scratch and private logs, including a holdout author's scratch, are readable from gate commands. This predates the diff: gates were never denied temp reads. The diff's docs now say the implementer harness can read other invocations' scratch, but do not say gates can. The issue scope does not require denying temp, so this is a documented gap rather than a regression.
findings.suggestion: Either deny the shared temp parent for gates, allowing only this run's scratch (the scratch is already in allowRead), or name this gap explicitly in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md under the gate read rules.
findings.failure_scenario: A holdout author writes scenario text into its scratch under /var/folders/.../T/lr-*/claude-501. A candidate's gate command running in parallel lists the temp parent and reads that file.

findings.title: A readable credential store in an editor is reported as a write-profile failure
findings.detail: In sandboxProbe, when a denied credential read succeeds under an editing profile, the probe returns WRITE_NOT_ENFORCED ('write profile not enforced'). A read-confinement failure in the Codex editor is therefore reported as a write failure, and runCodex surfaces 'Codex write confinement not verified'. The reason is misleading for operators diagnosing a read leak.
findings.suggestion: Add a READ_NOT_ENFORCED reason (or reuse NOT_ENFORCED) for the probeReads path, and keep WRITE_NOT_ENFORCED for the write canaries.
findings.failure_scenario: ~/.ssh is readable under the Codex editor profile because of a profile regression. The editor refuses to run, but the error reads 'write confinement not verified', which sends the operator to the wrong part of the profile.

findings.title: Tests call runConfined and writeRoots without scoping HOME, so they depend on the real credential paths
findings.detail: Several tests call runConfined or writeRoots with no readPolicyScope, so resolvedHome() returns the real home and policySpellings stats real credential paths. Under the Bash sandbox, where ~/.ssh gives EPERM on stat, these tests fail with 'Cannot resolve read policy path ~/.ssh' (4 in sandbox.test.ts, 14 in scratch.test.ts). With HOME overridden to an empty directory they pass. The failures are environmental, but they show the tests depend on the developer's real home. The EPERM is also treated as fatal, which is fail-closed as intended but makes results depend on the account's permissions.
findings.suggestion: Wrap every test that reaches the policy in readPolicyScope.run({ home: <temp> }) so no test touches the real HOME, as the newer tests already do.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer or CI host whose ~/.ssh cannot be stat'ed by the test process runs the sandbox suite, and roughly 18 tests fail for reasons unrelated to the change.

findings.title: Source change is well over the stated budget
findings.detail: The issue budgets about 150 changed source lines plus tests. The source diff is 233 added and 36 removed lines across src (read-policy.ts alone is 127), before counting the rework of codex.ts's probe and the ConfinementError relocation. This is scope creep against the stated budget, not a functional defect.
findings.suggestion: Trim what the issue does not need: the ConfinementError move, the probeReads restructuring, and the unused home option in ReadPolicyOptions. Or record the overrun and its reason in the PR description.
findings.failure_scenario: Reviewers cannot tell which lines are required by #487 and which are side effects, so review of the trust-boundary code gets harder.

output.summary: Checked the gate and editor read policy in src/harness/read-policy.ts, scratch.ts, sandbox.ts, codex.ts and claude.ts against the request. The core mechanism is sound: gates get a home-wide read deny with a checkout, scratch, Git and toolchain allowlist, the overlap check fails closed, and the editors get the credential denies through the existing denyRead plumbing. Real Seatbelt probes exist for the gate boundary, ssh, the Claude outer editor and the Codex editor. Running the suites in a throwaway copy with a fresh install and a neutral HOME gave 384 pass, 15 skip (nested sandbox-exec is unavailable in this session, so every Seatbelt-backed test was skipped), and 2 environmental failures from EPERM on /private/tmp. Biome is clean. The allowlist is still wrong in three places: it allows the cargo home whole, so crates.io tokens are readable by every gate and editor; a relocated factory data dir and the shared temp directory stay readable to gates, which contradicts the request. Source changes total about 233 lines against a 150-line budget.

findings.title: Gate allowlist exposes cargo credential files (crates.io token) to every gate
findings.detail: homeReadPolicy adds the whole cargo home (process.env.CARGO_HOME ?? ~/.cargo) to allowRead. The gate profile therefore contains (deny file-read* home) followed by (allow file-read* (subpath ".../.cargo")). Nothing re-denies ~/.cargo/credentials or ~/.cargo/credentials.toml: they are not in the credentials list, and privateReadPaths() only returns the SQLite database and its sidecars. I built the policy with a stand-in home containing .cargo/credentials.toml: the emitted profile allows that file, and the deny-rule list contains no cargo entry. Editors have no protection either, because the editor credential list omits cargo. cargo login stores the registry token there, so any gate's candidate code (a build script, a test, a malicious crate) can read and exfiltrate it.
findings.suggestion: Deny the cargo credential files inside the allowed cargo home. Put them in the denyRead set (like privateReadPaths), not in the overlap-checked credentials list: adding them to credentials would make every gate on a machine with cargo fail its overlap check. Also add them to the editor credential list. A narrower allowance (cargo bin and config files only) would also work. Add a real-Seatbelt test: head -c 1 on a stand-in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml must fail for a gate and for an editor.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate runs a candidate's test script on a machine where the owner has run cargo login. The script runs `cat "$CARGO_HOME/credentials.toml"` (or reads ~/.cargo/credentials.toml directly) and sends it over HTTPS. The allowlist permits the read because it covers the whole cargo home.

findings.title: Relocated factory data directory is not denied to gates
findings.detail: The gate home-wide deny applies only to $HOME. paths.runs is join(home, "runs"), and LIMITLESS_HOME or overrides.home can place the data directory anywhere (config.ts:143). configureReadPolicy receives only configDir (config.ts:315), so the data home is never added to the gate's denyRead. I checked this with home=<tmp>/home and a checkout at <tmp>/srv/runs/eval/worktree: another run's checkout at <tmp>/srv/runs/other/worktree gets no deny rule, and the deny list contains only the home and its credential subpaths. The request requires that other runs' checkouts and the factory data directory fall outside the gate's reads, and that holds only when the data directory sits under home.
findings.suggestion: Pass paths.home into the read policy and deny it for gates, with the same allowRead re-grants the run already gets (checkout, scratch, Git paths, toolchains). Add a test that uses a data directory outside the fake home and asserts the deny rule covers it.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator sets LIMITLESS_HOME=/srv/limitless. A gate for run A runs candidate code that does `head -c 1 /srv/limitless/runs/B/worktree/...` and reads run B's checkout, or the factory's database beside it.

findings.title: Gates can still read other invocations' scratch and logs in the shared temp directory
findings.detail: The gate's deny list is home, credentials and the database only. createScratch puts every invocation's scratch under /private/tmp/lr-*/claude-501 (candidates are /tmp, then TMPDIR), and the gate profile has no deny for those paths. Concurrent runs therefore leave their scratch readable to a gate's candidate code. That includes a holdout author's scratch file, which the ARCHITECTURE residual-risk note says can hold scenario text, and runConfined's copy of ~/.cargo/config.toml, which can contain registry tokens. privateReadRoots() already lists these temp roots for confined readers, but the gate policy does not use it.
findings.suggestion: Deny the shared temp roots for gates (privateReadRoots() minus the run's own scratch, which the allowRead re-grant covers). Verify that the run's own scratch stays readable and that a sibling scratch fails.
findings.failure_scenario: A holdout author writes scenario text into its scratch while a gate runs the implementer's tests. The candidate's test reads /private/tmp/lr-<holdout>/claude-501/<file> and returns the scenarios.

findings.title: Path-based read denies can be bypassed with a hard link into the checkout (unverified under Seatbelt)
findings.detail: The profile denies reads by path and grants writes to the checkout. A hard link to a denied credential file, created inside the checkout, would be readable through the allowed path because the inode is the same. The profile has no file-link restriction. I confirmed that the link is possible in this environment: a 0600 file owned by the same user can be hard-linked into another directory and read there (ln succeeded). I could not check the Seatbelt behaviour, because nested sandbox-exec returns sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted here. The database-only denies predate this change, but the new home-wide and credential denies rely on the same path-only mechanism.
findings.suggestion: Check whether Seatbelt's file-link operation applies to the source path. If it does, deny file-link* on the home and credential subpaths. Add a real-Seatbelt test: ln <stand-in credential> <checkout>/alias must fail, or head of the alias must fail.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate's candidate code runs `ln ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ./k && head -c 1 ./k`. If the link is permitted, the key is read through the checkout's read allowance.

findings.title: Home resolution follows $HOME, not the password database that ssh uses
findings.detail: resolvedHome uses os.homedir(), which Bun resolves from $HOME (verified: HOME=<x> makes homedir() return <x>). The request says ssh finds keys through the password database. If the factory process runs with a HOME that differs from the account's home, the home-wide deny and the credential list cover the wrong directory, while the real ~/.ssh stays readable. I could not confirm a passwd lookup that disagrees with HOME, because Bun's userInfo() also follows HOME.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the password-database home directly (for example through a native lookup), or refuse to start when HOME differs from it, and document the choice.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon starts with HOME=/tmp/sandbox-home. The policy denies /tmp/sandbox-home/.ssh, while ssh run by the gate reads /Users/owner/.ssh through getpwuid.

findings.title: Sandbox-count assertion narrowed to a filter, so probe count depends on the host
findings.detail: The assertion on fake.sandboxes() now counts only commands containing the write-probe text. Editor probes also read each existing credential store (sandbox.ts and codex.ts use filter(existsSync)), and the fixture does not set a home scope, so the host's real home decides how many probes run. The later attempts-relative assertions hide that. The change weakens the count check and makes it host-dependent.
findings.suggestion: Set readPolicyScope to a temporary home in this test so the probe set is fixed, then assert the full count again.
findings.failure_scenario: On a machine without ~/.ssh the probe runs one fewer read, and on a machine with it, one more. The test passes either way, so a regression that adds or drops probes goes unnoticed.

findings.title: Source change is about 233 lines against a 150-line budget
findings.detail: git diff --numstat for src/ gives 2+3+38+127+28+35 added lines (about 233), against the request's budget of about 150 source lines. The extra lines are mainly the overlap and spelling logic in read-policy.ts, the Git-path validation in scratch.ts, and the probe refactor in codex.ts.
findings.suggestion: Trim the non-essential code paths, or note the overrun in the PR description. Keep the single allowlist and the single credential list the request asked for.
findings.failure_scenario: Not a runtime defect. The review budget for the change is exceeded.

output.summary: Reviewed the executor seam diff (src/gates/executor.ts, gate-execution.ts, run.ts, engine.ts, land/queue.ts, config.ts, context.ts) against the request. Ran typecheck (clean), biome (one pre-existing warning outside the diff), and the gate, executor, gate-feedback, config-routing, land, pipeline and baseline-cache suites from a TMPDIR copy. Most of the suite passes. Two areas fail review. First, the change removes the RunContext constructor's whole-state redaction (context.ts:307), and the existing legacy-redaction test was edited to assert the opposite. Running the original test against the new code fails with the raw credential present in context.state. Second, the spec's "restart calls attach, not start" rule is only implemented for the first execution of a stage; regression retries, timeout re-runs and baseline retries are restarted instead, and tests assert that. Sandbox-only failures, not counted as findings: six pipeline-verification loopback tests fail with EPERM listen 127.0.0.1:0, and six auditDiff tests fail with "Cannot read private-strings.txt" because ~/.config/limitless is denied. Both pass or were not affected when re-run with LIMITLESS_CONFIG_DIR set to an empty dir (auditDiff) or are unverifiable here (loopback). One gate-executor forgotten-execution case failed once in a combined run and passed in every later run, so it is a possible flake.

findings.title: Run state is no longer sanitized on load, so legacy gate output with credentials stays raw in memory and is re-saved
findings.detail: The base RunContext constructor ran `this.state = redactGateData(this.state)` on every load, which sanitizes historical gate output, including credential-bearing output stored before the redaction fixes. The change deletes that line and only redacts a few fields at write time (baseline in prepare, lastGates, gateEvidence inputs, timeout artifacts). Fields such as `feedback`, `terminalReason`, `baseline` and `preRebaseGates` loaded from pre-existing rows are no longer sanitized. ctx.save() writes `this.state` back, so the raw secret is re-persisted on the next save. The removal is unexplained in the request and is not part of the executor seam.
findings.suggestion: Restore `this.state = redactGateData(this.state);` in the RunContext constructor. If its cost or a JSON-roundtrip side effect is the reason for removing it, scope that fix separately and keep the load-time sanitization guarantee.
findings.failure_scenario: A run that failed before this change stored gate output containing a token (e.g. `synthetic-legacy-gate-credential-421`) in `feedback`/`terminalReason`/`baseline`. After upgrade the daemon reopens the run with new RunContext(...); context.state still holds the raw token and the next ctx.save() writes it back unredacted. Verified: the original test/gate-feedback.test.ts 'legacy gate results are redacted on reopened state...' run against HEAD fails, with JSON.stringify(context.state) containing the raw credential.

findings.title: Existing redaction test was edited to pass: its reopened-state redaction assertion was removed and an opposite assertion added
findings.detail: The test title changed from 'legacy gate results are redacted on reopened state, checkpoints, HTTP and SSE reads' to '...without altering run state'. The `JSON.stringify(context.state)` entry that asserted the reopened state contains '[redacted]' was deleted from the messages list (around line 228), and `expect(context.state).toEqual(state)` (line 173) asserts the raw state is kept. The test was weakened to match the removed sanitization, which the rubric treats as test gaming.
findings.suggestion: Restore the original test assertions and the constructor sanitization (see the previous finding). If the behaviour is meant to change, state that explicitly in the request and in the report, then update the assertion to the new intended contract, not the other way around.
findings.failure_scenario: Any future regression that leaks raw legacy gate output through reopened run state now passes this test. Against the original test file, HEAD fails on the reopened state, so the edit is what hides the regression.

findings.title: Restarted regression retries, timeout re-runs and baseline retries are started again instead of attached
findings.detail: The request requires that a restart between start and result calls attach and not start, and that a stored handle identifies the work. runGateExecution only reuses a stored handle for purposes baseline, initial and rebase. For regression-retry, timeout and baseline-retry the handle is dropped (cancelGateExecution + clear state) and the whole stage starts again, including initial. test/gate-executor.test.ts (restart reattaches... test) asserts `fresh.starts` has length 2 and `attaches` does not contain the handle for these purposes. The deviation is commented ('later attempts depend on its setup') but is not in the request or the report, and the implementer's report is empty.
findings.suggestion: Either attach to every persisted purpose (the local executor already re-runs an attached check with the same request), or get explicit sign-off that only first executions are resumable and record that in the request. The tests should then reflect the chosen contract.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is killed while a 900s timeout re-run is in flight. On restart the stage runs the full initial gates again (starts a new execution), instead of attaching to the in-flight timeout run, so gate work is repeated and the regression/timeout bookkeeping differs from the attach path the spec asked for.

findings.title: Resumed prepare skips the baseline cache, which the request says must not change
findings.detail: The baseline cache read is now skipped whenever `ctx.state.gateExecution?.stage === "prepare"`, so a resumed prepare always runs its baseline even when a passing cache entry exists. The request says the baseline cache does not change. This is an unlisted behaviour change in the cache path.
findings.suggestion: Drop the stage check, or justify it in a comment and in the report, and add a test for the cache-hit-on-resume case.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts during prepare with a valid cache entry for the base commit. The baseline runs again, taking the full gate time, instead of reusing the cache.

findings.title: Run with no stored handle starts on the injected executor, not on local as the request requires
findings.detail: executeGate forces a local executor only when a stored handle is local and the injected executor is not. With no stored handle, it uses the injected executor. The request says runs that predate the change, with no handle, resume on local. The current config only accepts local, so this is latent, but a LAN or GitHub executor would route legacy runs elsewhere.
findings.suggestion: Make the no-stored-handle resume path explicitly local (the caller knows whether a stage is resuming), and test it with a non-local injected fake.
findings.failure_scenario: After a LAN executor is added and selected, a run interrupted before this change (no gateExecution in state) resumes its gates on the LAN executor, not on local.

findings.title: Interface and request deviate from the spec signature without explanation
findings.detail: The request specifies attach(handle, signal) and Req = { repo, baseSha, headSha, gates, checks }. The code has attach(handle, signal, req?, hooks?) and adds a required `cwd` to GateRequest. The extra arguments are probably needed for local re-runs, but the implementer's report is empty, so the deviation is undocumented. ExecutionEvent also has an unused 'status' variant and kind union entries for backends that do not exist yet.
findings.suggestion: Document the deviation next to the interface (why local needs the request on re-attach), drop unused variants, and keep the kind union to the kinds that exist.
findings.failure_scenario: A future executor author implements attach from the spec signature and gets a type error or a silent missing request, because the required request is only passed through an optional parameter.

findings.title: Diff exceeds the ~200-line budget and adds unrequested behaviour
findings.detail: Source changes total roughly 475 lines (executor.ts 197, gate-execution.ts 67, run.ts ~106, engine.ts ~67, queue.ts 26, plus smaller edits), against an 'about 200 changed source lines' budget and 'no new behaviour beyond the seam'. Unrequested changes include redacting the gate-config log line, redacting timeout artifacts and rebase artifacts, redacting onResult events, and the cache bypass above. Several are good fixes but they are outside the seam refactor.
findings.suggestion: Split out the redaction and cache changes, or describe them in the PR as separate behaviour changes.
findings.failure_scenario: A reviewer cannot separate the refactor from the new redaction behaviour, so a regression in either one is hard to bisect.

findings.title: Forgotten-execution test depends on global gate-slot state and a 5s pid poll; one failure was seen in a combined run
findings.detail: The 'forgotten local execution stops before replacement' test asserts `gateSlots.snapshot().occupied` (process-wide) and polls a child pid with a 5s deadline. It failed once when run in a four-file batch with the other gate and pipeline suites, and passed in three standalone runs and in a gates+executor pair. The failure text was not captured, so I could not confirm the cause.
findings.suggestion: Make the slot and child-process assertions local to the test (own gateSlots instance or a per-test slot cap), and raise or remove the 5s spawn deadline.
findings.failure_scenario: Under a loaded CI runner or with another test holding a gate slot, the occupancy assertion or the pid deadline fails intermittently, blocking merges for an unrelated reason.

findings.title: executeGate takes four optional positional parameters, which is hard to read at call sites
findings.detail: executeGate(req, signal, hooks, injected, stored, persist, onSettled) has four trailing optional positional arguments. Callers in the engine, land queue and gate-execution pass several of them, and the defaults are non-obvious (e.g. `injected` undefined means a new local executor on every call, which loses the shared live registry).
findings.suggestion: Take one options object (executor, stored handle, persist, onSettled) so each call names its fields.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `stored` in the `injected` slot, the types still accept it, and the run silently starts fresh instead of resuming.

output.summary: The executor seam is sound: executeGate persists the handle before attach, attach after restart re-runs without calling start, cancel is idempotent, and typecheck and biome pass on the changed files. Two defects block merge. First, the diff removes the load-time whole-state credential redaction in RunContext and rewrites the legacy-redaction test to assert the raw state is kept; a probe confirms a credential in persisted state now survives reopen and is written back raw (base writes [redacted]). Second, the change is about 475 source lines against the ~200-line budget and adds behaviour beyond the seam. Test results: gate-executor, gate-feedback and gates pass except six auditDiff tests, which fail on base too (the sandbox cannot read ~/.config/limitless/private-strings.txt). land-queue and pipeline-gates pass. Three baseline-cache timeouts, ten loopback-verification failures and the preview cancel test also fail on base, so they are environmental. Not run to completion: config-routing, the remaining failure-injection, delivery-restart, review-restart and gate-evidence files.

findings.title: Legacy-redaction test weakened to assert raw in-memory state
findings.detail: The test previously checked that the reopened context's serialized state contained [redacted] and no secret (JSON.stringify(context.state) was one of the checked messages). The diff removes that message and adds expect(context.state).toEqual(state), which requires the raw legacy secret to remain in memory. The test was renamed to match ('without altering run state'). The redaction guarantee is now untested, and the test enshrines the regression.
findings.suggestion: Restore the assertion that serialized reopened state contains no secret and does contain [redacted]. If the constructor redaction is intentionally removed, that needs a separate justification and a test asserting the new behaviour, not an edit that makes the old guarantee disappear.
findings.failure_scenario: A run whose persisted state contains a credential that was not registered when it was written is reopened. The test still passes while context.state holds the raw credential, and any later ctx.save writes it back.

findings.title: Load-time redaction of the whole run state was removed
findings.detail: The base constructor ends with this.state = redactGateData(this.state), which scrubs every string in the reloaded run state. The diff deletes that line and adds targeted redaction only at a few gate sites in engine.ts. Non-gate fields (feedback, answers, terminalReason, toolCommands and others) are no longer scrubbed on load. Probe: a run state with a registered credential in feedback, reopened and then saved. Base: in-memory and persisted value are both '[redacted]'. HEAD: in-memory and persisted value are both the raw secret.
findings.suggestion: Restore this.state = redactGateData(this.state) in the RunContext constructor, or justify its removal and cover every state write path with redaction. Keep the new gate-site redactions if they are still wanted.
findings.failure_scenario: A credential that was not registered when stored (for example, a token added to secrets later) sits in run state. After a daemon restart, the run reloads it raw, the next ctx.save writes it back raw, and any path that does not re-redact (prompt builders, logs, or later persistence) can emit it.

findings.title: Change is about 2.4x the requested line budget and adds behaviour beyond the seam
findings.detail: The request budgets about 200 changed source lines plus tests and says 'no new behaviour beyond the seam'. The diff changes about 475 source lines (executor.ts 197 new, run.ts 106, engine.ts 67, gate-execution.ts 67, queue.ts 26, plus small edits), and about 870 test lines. Behaviour changes beyond the seam include: redaction of results passed to onResult (so the land log now writes redacted output instead of raw); redaction of the timeout artifact, the comparison artifacts and the prepare log line; gate results to onResult now delivered through an async iterator rather than synchronously; and a new durable gateExecution field with a checkpoint. AGENTS.md treats line budget overruns as a reason to cut the change back.
findings.suggestion: Split out the executor seam, the local executor and routing; drop the extra redaction and log-content changes unless they are separately justified; keep only what the request requires for behaviour to stay identical.
findings.failure_scenario: Review and merge of a ~475-line change for a stated ~200-line refactor, with output and checkpoint behaviour changes that the request excludes.

findings.title: Executor interface deviates from the specified attach(handle, signal) and declares unimplemented kinds
findings.detail: The request specifies attach(handle, signal) returning an Execution. The implementation adds optional req and hooks parameters, which the local executor needs after a restart but a remote executor would not. The kind union also lists 'github-actions', 'lan' and 'claude-cloud', which do not exist in this slice.
findings.suggestion: Document why req and hooks are on attach (or move them onto the handle or a context object), and narrow kind to 'local' until the next slice adds the other kinds.
findings.failure_scenario: A future remote executor must accept an unused request argument, and the kind union has to be edited when each backend lands.

findings.title: Circular import between run.ts and executor.ts
findings.detail: run.ts imports executeGate from executor.ts, and executor.ts imports runLocalGates from run.ts. Both are used lazily, so this works today, but the cycle is a trap for module-initialisation changes.
findings.suggestion: Move runLocalGates and its helpers into a module that executor.ts imports, or keep the compatibility runGates wrapper in a separate module so run.ts does not import the executor.
findings.failure_scenario: A module-level use of either export during initialisation, added later, would see an undefined binding.

findings.title: starts entry leaks when persist throws after start
findings.detail: localExecutor.start stores {request, signal} in starts. The entry is deleted only when the attached run finishes. If persist throws in executeGate (line 160) before attach, the entry stays in a Map that lives for the whole Factory.
findings.suggestion: Remove the entry in executeGate when persist or attach throws, or have start register the entry only after persist succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated ctx.save failures during gate start grow the starts map by one request and signal each time.

findings.title: A stored handle of an unknown kind leaves the stage stuck on every resume
findings.detail: If a stored handle has a kind other than the injected executor's, executeGate throws 'Unavailable gate executor' before onSettled. runGateExecution's finally sees settled=false and leaves gateExecution in place, so each resume throws at the same point. This cannot happen in the current release, which only creates local handles, but a rollback from a release that writes other kinds would hit it.
findings.suggestion: When the stored kind is not available, cancel and clear the pending handle and start the work afresh on the current executor, as the purpose-mismatch path already does.
findings.failure_scenario: A handle with kind 'lan' written by a newer release is read by this release. Every resume of that stage throws 'Unavailable gate executor: lan'.

output.summary: Reviewed the change against #487 by reading the diff and the surrounding code (read-policy.ts, sandbox.ts, scratch.ts, codex.ts, claude.ts, the entry-point scope wiring, docs and tests), and by running the targeted suites in a TMPDIR copy of HEAD (the worktree had no node_modules and the resolved zod was the wrong major). Results: 570 tests, 533 pass, 18 skip, 19 fail. Those 19 are environmental where checked: the review sandbox denies ~/.ssh and ~/.config/limitless and blocks /tmp writes; with a stand-in HOME and LIMITLESS_CONFIG_DIR, gates.test.ts passes fully and scratch.test.ts fails only 2 tests that fail identically on the base commit. A failure-injection rerun gave 111 pass and 21 fail, all 'barrier timed out'; I confirmed the base commit fails one of those cancel tests, but did not check the other 20 against base, so they remain unattributed. Real-Seatbelt probes could not run (nested sandbox-exec is refused here), so the spec's real-probe claims are unverified. Fail-closed handling for an unresolvable home and for allowlist/credential overlap is implemented and tested, the ssh identity test exists (sandbox.test.ts:242), and every entry point that runs gates or editors is inside a read-policy scope. The request is not met for the gate and editor boundary: the gate deny is narrower than the reader's private roots, cross-run scratch remains readable (including a factory-copied cargo config), and hard links may bypass the path-based denies. Changes are needed before merge.

findings.title: Path-based read denies can be bypassed with a hard link into a writable root
findings.detail: The profile denies file-write* and reads by path only (`(deny file-read* (subpath …))`). `file-link` is a separate Seatbelt operation that the profile never denies, and linking needs no read rule on the source. A candidate or editor can run `ln ~/.ssh/id_rsa <checkout>/k` (or ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, ~/.codex/auth.json) and then `head -c1 <checkout>/k`. The read matches the checkout allow rule, so the credential is readable. The same applies to the Claude editor (which only denies credential stores) and the Codex editor. The mechanism predates this change for the database sidecars, but the new credential and home denies depend on it. Not measured here because nested sandbox-exec is refused in this session.
findings.suggestion: Add `(deny file-link …)` over every denied root (home for gates, the credential list for editors), then re-allow file-link under the allowed roots. Allow linking from the bun install cache and cargo registry if their installers hard-link. Add a real probe: `ln "$HOME/.ssh/<file>" "$PWD/x"` must fail with a permission error, and so must a read of the link.
findings.failure_scenario: Gate candidate runs `ln ~/.config/limitless/secrets.env ./leak && cat ./leak`. The link succeeds (no file-link deny). The read of ./leak matches (allow file-read* subpath checkout), so the secret is printed into the gate log or sent over HTTPS.

findings.title: Gate home-wide deny leaves the factory data directory and other runs' checkouts readable when they live outside $HOME
findings.detail: For gates the only home-wide rule is `denyRead` on $HOME (line 179), plus the credential list and privateReadPaths() (the database and sidecars). LIMITLESS_HOME (config.ts:144) can point anywhere, for example /Volumes/… or /opt/…. In that layout, another run's checkout under <home>/runs/<other>/worktree, the work and repos trees, and any non-database files under the data directory stay readable by a gate. The existing reader policy already denies privateReadRoots() (scratch.ts:189: /Users, /Volumes, /var/folders, /private/tmp, tmpdir, /tmp), and the request asks that the factory data directory and other runs' checkouts fall outside the gate's reads. Only the database is protected in this layout.
findings.suggestion: Reuse privateReadRoots() for gate denyRead, as the reader does. The allowRead entries (cwd, scratch, Git paths, toolchains) already take precedence, and the overlap check already refuses conflicts. Alternatively, refuse to start a gate when LIMITLESS_HOME or paths.runs lies outside the home directory unless it is explicitly listed. Add a test where the data directory sits outside the stand-in home.
findings.failure_scenario: Operator sets LIMITLESS_HOME=/Volumes/data/limitless. A gate for run A runs `cat /Volumes/data/limitless/runs/B/worktree/.env`, reading run B's checkout and any secret stored there. The home-wide deny does not match /Volumes.

findings.title: Other runs' scratch stays readable to gates, and the factory copies cargo config into it
findings.detail: Command scratch is created under /tmp or TMPDIR (scratch.ts:32, `candidates = ["/tmp", tmpdir()]`) and is outside the home-wide deny. The gate profile is `allow default` for reads outside home, so one gate can read another invocation's scratch. runConfined also copies the operator's ~/.cargo/config and config.toml into scratch (sandbox.ts:251). Cargo configuration can carry registry tokens, so the copy places a credential in a location every concurrent gate can read. The change adds no deny for other scratch. ARCHITECTURE.md now calls this a residual risk for the implementer, but gates are not covered by that note, and the request's intent was that other runs' data fall outside gate reads.
findings.suggestion: Deny privateReadRoots() for gates (as in the reader) and allow only the run's own scratch, or make scratch private per run with a per-run allow. Do not copy token-bearing cargo configuration into shared-readable scratch; copy only the non-credential settings, or point cargo at the real config read-only through an environment variable.
findings.failure_scenario: Two gates run concurrently. Run A's setup copies ~/.cargo/config.toml, which contains a `[registries.x] token`, into /private/tmp/limitless-…/cargo/config.toml. Run B's candidate code runs `cat /private/tmp/limitless-*/cargo/config.toml` and gets the token.

findings.title: Ancestor literal grants re-allow home-level package.json, bunfig.toml, tsconfig.json and jsconfig.json for gates
findings.detail: ancestorReadPolicy adds literal read grants for these four names in every ancestor of each allowed path, which includes $HOME itself. That re-allows `~/bunfig.toml` (bunfig.toml can hold registry tokens) and the other three, which the home-wide deny is meant to cover. The request says a file directly under the home directory must be denied. The test at sandbox.test.ts:69 asserts these grants, and GUIDE.md discloses them, so this is a design choice that contradicts the request and is not needed for the stated toolchain paths. Bun reads its global config from ~/.bunfig.toml, which is still denied, so practical exposure is limited.
findings.suggestion: Drop the literal manifest grants from the home ancestor, or limit them to paths below the checkout and toolchain roots. If bun or tsc needs them for discovery, verify the minimum with a real probe and document it.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate's candidate runs `cat ~/bunfig.toml` and reads a token-bearing registry configuration that the home deny was supposed to block.

findings.title: Source change is about 370 lines against a request budget of about 150, with machinery the request did not ask for
findings.detail: Source additions total about 370 lines: a new 211-line read-policy.ts that includes ancestor metadata and literal grants, an allowRead plumbing path in WriteRoots, a rewritten policySpellings replacing spellings(), a snapshot of 15 credential-location environment variables, and a probeReads refactor in codex.ts. The request asked for one short allowlist and one reuse of the denyRead plumbing, and said to add nothing in parallel to it. Much of the extra complexity is what made the literal grants and the metadata rules necessary.
findings.suggestion: Trim to the requested list and the one denyRead path. Remove the ancestor literal and metadata machinery if the discovery issue is verified as not needed, and keep the env snapshot to the variables the request names.
findings.failure_scenario: Future maintainers cannot tell which ancestor and literal rules are required for a given toolchain, so an allow rule widens by accident when a toolchain changes.

findings.title: Editing-mode read-probe failure is reported as 'write profile not enforced'
findings.detail: In probeReads, when a read denial fails for an editing spec, the code returns WRITE_NOT_ENFORCED ("write profile not enforced"). The actual failure is a read that should have been denied. The probe still fails closed, but the reason an operator sees is wrong, which makes a read-policy regression look like a write-policy regression.
findings.suggestion: Add a READ_NOT_ENFORCED ConfinementFailure ("read profile not enforced") and use it when `editing` is true and a denied read succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: The Codex editor profile stops denying ~/.codex. The run is refused with 'write profile not enforced', and an operator looks at write settings instead of the read deny list.

findings.title: Real-probe tests cannot detect outside-home data directories, temp scratch or hard links
findings.detail: The gate home-boundary test (sandbox.test.ts:~150) puts the stand-in home at `root`, so the factory data directory and sibling checkouts are under home by construction. No test sets the data directory or runs outside home, checks other scratch in TMPDIR, or checks that `ln` from a credential path into the checkout fails. These are the gaps findings 1 to 3 describe, so the suite would pass with them present.
findings.suggestion: Add real-probe cases: a data directory outside the stand-in home, another invocation's scratch under TMPDIR, and a hard link from a denied credential path into the checkout. Each must be denied, and each test should be skipIf(seatbeltSkip).
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that drops the privateReadRoots deny for gates still passes every listed test.

output.summary: Reviewed the change against #487's four requirements and rubric. The core design holds up on reading: gates get a home-wide read deny with a short allowlist (checkout, scratch, recorded git paths, bun/cargo/rustup subpaths, configured toolchains); both editor profiles deny the listed credential stores through one module (read-policy.ts); overlap and unresolved-home cases fail closed before launch; and the Seatbelt rule ordering (deny home, allow run paths, re-deny specific credential paths) is consistent. Gate, editor and eval entry points all set the read-policy and confinement scopes. The main problem is that the Codex editor leaves Claude's login readable and the tests assert that. Other findings are minor. Verification limits: nested sandbox-exec is refused in this session, so the real-Seatbelt probes were skipped (test/sandbox.test.ts: 16 pass, 12 skip, 0 fail), and enforcement claims are backed only by reading and profile-text tests. In a $TMPDIR copy of HEAD with locked dependencies, test/scratch.test.ts gave 83 pass, 4 skip, 9 fail. Seven of the nine are "Cannot resolve read policy path ~/.ssh", caused by this session's Bash sandbox denying ~/.ssh reads, and two come from sandbox write limits. Those are not product verdicts. In the worktree itself, scratch.test.ts does not load because no node_modules is installed there. I did not run the real Codex or Claude CLI probes, and I did not review Keychain access, which the issue lists as out of scope.

findings.title: Codex editor can read Claude's login store (~/.claude, ~/.claude.json)
findings.detail: The editor deny list (credentials array, read-policy.ts:119-150) has no .claude or .claude.json entry, so the Codex editor profile leaves them readable. The test at test/scratch.test.ts:1493 asserts codexAccess(codex, ~/.claude/login) === 'read', which locks this in. The issue scopes the #369 gap to Claude editors only ('Name what stays readable to Claude editors (their own CLI login)'), and the report names no Codex-side gap. Codex never needs Claude's login. The Codex editor profile also sets network={enabled=true} (codex.ts:292), so a prompt-injected Codex editor can read the owner's Claude login and send it out.
findings.suggestion: Add .claude and .claude.json to the Codex-only deny (or to the shared list, since the Claude editor's own login is a documented exception and the Claude-side profile can keep its #369 carve-out). Flip the test assertion to 'none', and name the remaining Claude-editor exposure under #369 as the issue asks.
findings.failure_scenario: A prompt-injected Codex editor runs a shell command that reads ~/.claude/.credentials (or the ~/.claude.json state file) and posts it over HTTPS. The Codex editor profile allows the read and network is enabled, so the owner's Claude login is exposed.

findings.title: spellings() now throws on unreadable existing paths, where the base tolerated them
findings.detail: The base spellings() used existsSync(), which returns false on EPERM/EACCES and so kept only the lexical path. spellings() now delegates to policySpellings(paths) with denied=false, and canonical() rethrows any non-ENOENT error as ConfinementError. I confirmed this in a $TMPDIR script with a chmod-000 directory: base returns the lexical path, while the new code throws 'Cannot resolve read policy path ...'. Callers include runCodex's reader branch (codex.ts ~812, spellings(spec.denyRead)) and sandbox probes, so an unreadable denyRead entry now escapes as a thrown exception rather than a returned status. That is still fail-closed, but it changes the error contract, and it is the cause of the editor-probe test failures in an environment where ~/.ssh is unstatable.
findings.suggestion: Keep the base tolerance for denied entries: call policySpellings(paths, true) inside spellings(), or catch the error and return the lexical spelling for denied inputs. Add a test asserting that an unstatable denyRead entry yields a returned status, not a throw.
findings.failure_scenario: On a machine where a configured deny_read path (or ~/.ssh) returns EACCES to the factory process, runCodex throws ConfinementError out of the reader/editor path, not an 'unavailable' result. The editor-probe tests then fail with 'Cannot resolve read policy path ~/.ssh'.

findings.title: Shared test read policy uses the real home directory, making tests machine-dependent
findings.detail: testReadPolicy is configureReadPolicy(undefined, ...), which sets home to the real homedir(). Editor and probe tests therefore resolve the developer's real ~/.ssh, ~/.config/gh and similar paths. In this session, nine test/scratch.test.ts tests failed on those real paths, not on the code under test. The suite is not hermetic, and results depend on what the machine's home looks like.
findings.suggestion: Let tests construct a read policy with a temporary home (for example, an options override in configureReadPolicy or a helper that sets home), and use it in read-policy-support.ts and the editor/probe fixtures.
findings.failure_scenario: On a CI runner or developer machine where ~/.ssh or ~/.config/gh is unreadable or differently laid out, the editor-probe tests fail or pass for reasons unrelated to the change.

findings.title: A readable credential store in editing mode is reported as 'write profile not enforced'
findings.detail: In probeReads, when a read of a denied credential succeeds, the code returns result(editing ? WRITE_NOT_ENFORCED : NOT_ENFORCED). For editors this labels a read leak as a write failure. Operators get the wrong diagnosis for the failing rule, which matters when a credential store is exposed.
findings.suggestion: Add a READ_NOT_ENFORCED ConfinementFailure (for example 'read profile not enforced') for the editing case, and assert the reason in the editor-probe tests.
findings.failure_scenario: An editor profile that leaves ~/.ssh readable reports 'write profile not enforced', sending the operator to the write rules instead of the read rules.

findings.title: Editor deny list omits common plaintext credential stores and factory data
findings.detail: The issue's editor list is followed exactly, so this is spec-compliant. Still, editors have network access, and the list leaves these readable: ~/.git-credentials and ~/.config/git/credentials (a git-centric factory's most likely plaintext store), ~/.pypirc, ~/.gem/credentials, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.m2/settings.xml. It also leaves ~/.limitless/runs (other runs' checkouts) and ~/.limitless/repos (every cached repository's source) readable to editors. Gates are unaffected because they deny all of home.
findings.suggestion: At least add ~/.git-credentials and ~/.config/git/credentials to the shared list, since they cost nothing. Name the rest, including ~/.limitless/runs and repos for editors, as a known gap in the report.
findings.failure_scenario: A prompt-injected editor reads ~/.git-credentials (a plaintext token) or another run's checkout and sends it out, because the list does not name those paths.

findings.title: Path-based read denies may not stop hard links into the writable checkout (unverified)
findings.detail: The Seatbelt read rules match paths. A gate can write inside its checkout and may be able to create a hard link to a file under ~/.ssh (same uid, no read needed to call link()). Opening the link would then match the allowed checkout path and succeed. I could not test this: nested sandbox-exec is refused here, so the real-profile behavior is unknown. If the link is allowed, the fix is a link-operation deny for denied paths, if the profile supports one.
findings.suggestion: Under the real gate profile, run `ln ~/.ssh/<key> ./k && head -c 1 ./k` (against a stand-in key under a temporary home) and check whether the link succeeds and whether the read of the link is denied. If it succeeds, deny the link operation for denyRead paths and add a real-Seatbelt test.
findings.failure_scenario: A candidate's test script runs `ln` against a private key under ~/.ssh, then reads the link inside the checkout, bypassing the subpath deny. This is unverified.

findings.title: Allowed roots expose credential-bearing config files (git common dir config, ~/.cargo/config*)
findings.detail: The gate allowlist readable set includes the git common directory and ~/.cargo/config and config.toml, as the spec requires. Both can hold secrets: remote URLs with embedded tokens in the common dir's config, and registry tokens in cargo config. The base already copied cargo config into scratch, so the cargo exposure predates this change, but the explicit read allowance is new. The git config exposure follows from the spec's allowlist. Neither is named in the report.
findings.suggestion: Document the exposure in the GUIDE/ARCHITECTURE docs. Optionally, copy only the needed cargo keys into scratch and stop allowing the original config reads, and keep credentials out of the shared common-dir config.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate's test script runs `cat $(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/config` or `cat ~/.cargo/config.toml` and reads a remote URL or registry token embedded there.

findings.title: Source diff is well over the stated budget, and boolean positional arguments hurt readability
findings.detail: The issue budgets about 150 changed source lines. The source diff is 333 added and 38 removed, including a new 211-line module, a Codex probe restructure, a ConfinementError move, and docs. Much of it is needed, such as the ancestor literal grants that git and bun require under a home-wide deny. Separately, writeRoots(cwd, scratch, false, spec.denyRead) is repeated at four call sites with an unlabeled boolean.
findings.suggestion: Either state in the report why the budget was exceeded, or split out the probe restructure and the spellings rewrite. Replace the boolean with an options object, such as writeRoots(cwd, scratch, { gate: true, denyRead }).
findings.failure_scenario: Not a runtime failure; a future caller passes the wrong boolean and silently gets gate reads or editor reads.

findings.title: SSH probe passes -i explicitly, not the default identity lookup the issue measured
findings.detail: The issue's probe is `ssh -o BatchMode=yes <host> true`, with no -i, so ssh finds keys through the passwd database. The test passes -i to a stand-in key. The denial comes from the same subpath rule, so enforcement is probably correct, but the test does not exercise the path the issue reported.
findings.suggestion: Add a variant that uses HOME-independent default discovery (for example, a stand-in key at the default name under the temporary home, with no -i and no -F override), so the test covers the reported path.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that only affects default identity discovery (for example, an ssh config or getpwuid path) passes the existing test.

output.summary: Reviewed the diff for src/harness/sandbox.ts, src/pipeline/preview.ts and test/preview.test.ts against the request. The core change is sound: build, seed and serve now go through runConfined with the same write roots, read policy and Seatbelt probe as gates; the serve is started through runSandboxed with a started-token check; the daemon port is denied via the engine's confinement scope; the preview scratch is shared across steps and removed only after the serve has terminated; and launch or verification failures fail closed before the candidate runs. I found no blocker or major defect. Checks I could run: `bun test test/preview.test.ts` gave 2 pass, 1 skip (the nested-Seatbelt probe skip), and 21 fail. All 21 failures are `availablePort` failing with EPERM on listen, which this sandbox's local-binding restriction causes, so the server-backed, fake-confinement and env tests were not exercised. Lint and typecheck were not run because node_modules is not installed and I did not install it. I also confirmed with a small Bun script that an unhandled rejection is reported and exits 1.
