The existing restart tests only use a 'kill' fault, which never aborts the signal, so this path is untested. The spec requires 'a restart between start and result calls attach and not start'. For local the result is harmless because attach re-runs anyway, but for the seam's future remote executors a graceful restart would orphan the first execution and start a second one.
findings.suggestion: Only clear gateExecution when the execution actually completed with a result (or was cancelled by its own cancel path). On shutdown abort, keep the handle durable and skip the clear. Add a test that calls f.stop() while a fake execution is in flight, then asserts a resume calls attach, not start.
findings.failure_scenario: Daemon is stopped (SIGTERM / Factory.stop) during the gates stage with a remote-kind execution in flight. Stop aborts the run signal, executeGate cancels and settles, runGateExecution clears gateExecution and saves. On restart the resumed stage calls start() again, so a second remote job is started and the first is orphaned.

findings.title: Whole-state redaction on load was removed, so legacy gate output with credentials stays in run state and is written back on save
findings.detail: The base RunContext constructor ran this.state = redactGateData(this.state) (base line 307). That line is gone, and only baseline, cmp and lastGates are now redacted at write time. Legacy persisted state keeps raw gate output: feedback, terminalReason, preRebaseGates, lastVerifiedEvidence, gatesConfig and anything else already stored. Because save() writes this.state (src/pipeline/context.ts:362-373), the unredacted legacy values are persisted back to runs.state_json on the next checkpoint. HTTP responses still pass through redactGateData (src/server/http.ts:27), so the exposure is mainly the database and any path that reads state raw.
findings.suggestion: Restore the load-time redaction in the RunContext constructor (or redact on the path that reads the stored state), and keep the test that checks the reopened state is redacted.
findings.failure_scenario: A run created before this change has a gate result containing a credential (ANSI-split, as in the test) in feedback or preRebaseGates. The daemon reopens the run and checkpoints it. The credential is written back to the database in plaintext, where the previous code would have scrubbed it.

findings.title: Legacy redaction test was weakened to match the new behaviour instead of guarding it
findings.detail: The original test asserted that the reopened run state (JSON.stringify(context.state)) contains no secret, and that the checkpoint, HTTP and SSE reads redact it. The diff renames the test to 'without altering run state', replaces the redaction expectation with expect(context.state).toEqual(state) (line 173), and removes JSON.stringify(context.state) from the no-secret message list. Those edits make the test pass on the regressed behaviour, so nothing now detects reopened legacy state keeping secrets.
findings.suggestion: Revert the assertion change. Keep the redaction expectation for reopened state, or, if the removal is intentional, add a dedicated test that proves persisted state is redacted some other way. Do not change an assertion to match new output.
findings.failure_scenario: Reverting the constructor redaction (src/pipeline/context.ts) keeps this test green, because it now expects the raw state.

findings.title: Retry purposes are restarted on resume rather than reattached, which departs from the spec's restart rule
findings.detail: stored is set only for purposes baseline, initial and rebase (line 25). regression-retry, timeout and baseline-retry always start a new execution after a restart, and test/gate-executor.test.ts:516-570 asserts this. The spec says a restart between start and result calls attach and not start, and it names no exception. The code comment justifies the exception (retries depend on setup), and that is a reasonable design, but it is not disclosed in the implementer's report and it departs from the literal requirement.
findings.suggestion: Either make the exception explicit in the spec or the docs, or reattach retries and replay setup as the original stage would. Note the deviation in the PR description.
findings.failure_scenario: Restart while a regression-retry is pending: the retry is started again instead of attached, so the handle recorded before the restart is discarded.

findings.title: A stored handle of an unknown kind throws before settle and leaves gateExecution pending, so every resume fails
findings.detail: When stored.kind is not local and the injected executor is local, executeGate throws 'Unavailable gate executor' at line 158 before the try block. onSettled is never called, so runGateExecution (gate-execution.ts:62) does not clear gateExecution. Every resume matches the same stored handle and throws again. Nothing in this slice writes a non-local handle, so this matters only under version skew (a handle written by a newer executor, then a downgrade or a config change).
findings.suggestion: On an unavailable stored handle, clear it and fall through to start (or cancel it and surface an error that clears state), rather than leaving the durable record in place.
findings.failure_scenario: A future build stores a handle with kind 'lan'. The operator reverts to this build: the gates stage fails on every resume and cannot recover without manual DB edits.

findings.title: Diff is about 2.5x the ~200-line budget and includes behaviour changes outside the seam
findings.detail: Source additions and changes come to roughly 475 lines (executor.ts 197, run.ts 106, engine.ts 67, gate-execution.ts 67, queue.ts 26, plus small edits). The request asked for a refactor with no new behaviour beyond the seam. Beyond the seam, the change also redacts the prepare 'Gates' log line, redacts the events delivered to onResult (which changes what evals and the land log receive), moves the redaction of baseline and cmp into the engine, and removes the constructor redaction (see the security finding).
findings.suggestion: Split out the redaction changes into their own change, or revert them. Keep the seam limited to the executor, the routing and the handle durability.
findings.failure_scenario: Reviewing against the budget: the seam cannot be verified independently of the unrelated redaction behaviour changes.

findings.title: Executor kind union lists executors that do not exist; the attach signature differs from the spec; ExecutionEvent 'status' is unused
findings.detail: The kind type includes 'github-actions' | 'lan' | 'claude-cloud', none of which exist in this slice. attach takes (handle, signal, req?, hooks?), where the spec says attach(handle, signal); the extra req is needed for local resume, which is fine but should be stated. The 'status' ExecutionEvent variant is never produced.
findings.suggestion: Narrow kind to 'local' until the next executors land, and drop the unused status variant. Document why attach takes the request.
findings.failure_scenario: None at runtime; this is API surface that is not exercised.

output.summary: Review of the read-policy change (base d3e8014 to HEAD 5731023) is complete. Checks: generated profiles through writeRoots with temporary fixtures; confirmed a relocated factory data directory is not denied for gates, the editor deny list omits ~/.cloudflared, gate profiles leave /private/tmp readable, and a strict re-resolve in runCodex throws rather than reporting unavailable. Tests: sandbox, gates, harness, gate-evidence and gate-feedback suites gave 251 pass, 14 skip, 8 fail; scratch.test.ts gave 83 pass, 4 skip, 9 fail. All failures are sandbox-induced (EPERM on ~/.ssh, /tmp and ~/.limitless not writable). The failure-injection suite is unclassified: its hooks time out in the seed git helper, and the base-commit and full head-commit copy runs were stopped before completing. Real-Seatbelt probes could not run because nested sandbox-exec is refused here.

findings.title: Gate home deny ignores a relocated factory data directory
findings.detail: homeReadPolicy denies only options.home for gates (line 179). The factory data directory comes from paths.home, which loadConfig takes from LIMITLESS_HOME or overrides.home (src/config.ts:144) and is not passed into the read policy. When the data directory is outside $HOME, the gate profile has no deny for it, so another run's checkout (<data>/runs/<id>/worktree), work/, repos/ and logs stay readable to gate candidate code. I generated the profile with the data directory outside a temporary home: denyRead does not contain it, and no rule covers <data>/runs/other/worktree. The spec explicitly lists the factory's data directory and other runs' checkouts as falling outside the gate allowlist.
findings.suggestion: Carry the factory data directory (paths.home) in ReadPolicyOptions, deny it for gates alongside home, and allow only this run's checkout, scratch and recorded Git paths through the existing allowRead carve-outs. The overlap check must exempt the data directory itself, since the run's checkout sits inside it, and the DB must remain a specific deny. Add a real-Seatbelt test with a relocated LIMITLESS_HOME.
findings.failure_scenario: LIMITLESS_HOME=/Volumes/data/limitless. A candidate's gate command runs cat /Volumes/data/limitless/runs/<other-run>/worktree/.env. The gate profile has no deny for that path, so the read succeeds and leaks another run's files to candidate-controlled code.

findings.title: Editors can read the factory's own Cloudflare tunnel credentials
findings.detail: src/cli/service.ts:207-218 (tunnelConfig) reads ~/.cloudflared/<uuid>.json, the tunnel credentials file (it holds TunnelSecret), and writes limitless.yml that references it. The built-in editor credential list in homeReadPolicy (read-policy.ts ~lines 121-131) omits .cloudflared, so Claude and Codex editors can read it. Gates are protected only because they deny all of home. The same list also omits other plaintext stores such as ~/.git-credentials, ~/.config/git/credentials, ~/.pypirc, ~/.gem/credentials, ~/.m2/settings.xml, ~/.config/gcloud and ~/.azure.
findings.suggestion: Add .cloudflared to the built-in editor list (and document it in GUIDE.md), and consider the other common plaintext stores listed above. Keep the deny_read option for the rest.
findings.failure_scenario: A prompt-injected implementer (Claude editor, outer Seatbelt profile) runs cat ~/.cloudflared/<uuid>.json. Seatbelt does not deny it, the read succeeds, and the tunnel secret can leave the sandbox over the network.

findings.title: Gates can read other invocations' temporary files (scratch, holdout scenarios, logs)
findings.detail: privateReadRoots() treats /private/tmp and /private/var/folders as private, and confined readers deny them, but gate profiles deny only home. createScratch puts each invocation's scratch under /private/tmp/lr-*/claude-501, so a parallel run's scratch and logs are readable to candidate code in a gate. ARCHITECTURE.md (diff) says the holdout author writes into this shared directory during a run, so a candidate gate could read hidden scenario text from another run's scratch.
findings.suggestion: Deny the temporary roots (tmpdir(), /tmp, /private/var/folders, /private/tmp) for gates, with allowRead for this run's own scratch parent, as the readers' privateReadRoots already does. Or document explicitly that gate candidates can read other invocations' scratch.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A's holdout author writes scenario text into /private/tmp/lr-XYZ/claude-501/ during its run. Run B's candidate gate command runs cat /private/tmp/lr-XYZ/claude-501/*, reads the hidden scenarios, and tailors its code to them.

findings.title: Literal manifest grants leave ~/package.json and similar files readable to gates
findings.detail: ancestorReadPolicy adds literal file-read* allows for package.json, bunfig.toml, tsconfig.json and jsconfig.json in every ancestor of each allowed path, including the home directory, /Users, / and /private/tmp. Those literal allows come after the home-wide deny, so the profile lets a gate read $HOME/bunfig.toml and similar files. The profile output confirms (literal "<home>/package.json"), and the spec says a file directly under home must be denied.
findings.suggestion: Limit the literal manifest grants to ancestors strictly below home (or to the checkout's own ancestors), and state the exception in the docs if it is kept. Add a test that $HOME/bunfig.toml is denied.
findings.failure_scenario: A user keeps a registry token in ~/bunfig.toml. A gate candidate runs cat ~/bunfig.toml and reads it, because the literal grant overrides the home-wide deny.

findings.title: runCodex re-resolves the editor deny list strictly and throws instead of reporting unavailable
findings.detail: The editor deny list is computed with writeRoots(...).denyRead at lines 789-791, where the lenient resolver (denied=true) falls back to a lexical path on EACCES/EPERM. Line 812 then calls spellings(deny), which uses the strict resolver (denied=false) and throws ConfinementError for the same unresolvable credential path. In the test run this surfaced as an uncaught 'Cannot resolve read policy path ~/.ssh' from runCodex, instead of a status:'unavailable' result. The failure mode is fail-closed, but it is inconsistent with the rest of the editor path.
findings.suggestion: Use the same resolver in both places, or wrap the re-resolution so it returns an unavailable confinement result that names the path, as the other confinement failures do.
findings.failure_scenario: ~/.codex or ~/.ssh exists but the factory process cannot stat it (EPERM, for example under a restrictive ACL). runCodex throws ConfinementError from line 812 rather than returning an unavailable status, so the pipeline sees an operational exception instead of a clean confinement failure.

findings.title: Source change is well over the requested budget
findings.detail: The spec asks for about 150 changed source lines plus tests. The diff adds 338 source lines and deletes 40 (src and scripts). The largest parts are the new 211-line read-policy.ts, an AsyncLocalStorage scope threaded through five entry points (engine, evals runner, land queue, smoke), an environment snapshot of 15 variables, and ancestor literal and metadata machinery.
findings.suggestion: Trim non-essential machinery (the environment snapshot list, and ancestor literal and metadata grants where a simpler rule suffices), and consider whether the scope plumbing can reuse confinementScope.
findings.failure_scenario: Reviewers must audit about 340 new lines of policy logic, including AsyncLocalStorage propagation, to confirm the home-wide deny. A bug in the extra machinery is more likely to slip through.

findings.title: Unverified: hard link of a credential file into the writable checkout may bypass the read deny
findings.detail: Seatbelt's file-read* deny covers reads of a credential path, but link(2) is governed by a separate operation (file-link), which the profile does not restrict. If candidate code runs ln ~/.ssh/<key> ./k inside the writable checkout, the checkout allow may then let it read ./k, depending on whether Seatbelt checks the vnode's path or the name used to reach it. I could not test this because nested sandbox-exec is refused in this environment, so this is a risk to verify rather than a demonstrated bypass.
findings.suggestion: Run a real-Seatbelt probe under the gate profile: create a stand-in key under a temporary home, ln it into the checkout, and read the link. If it is readable, deny file-link (or the hard-link source) for credential paths, and add the probe as a test.
findings.failure_scenario: A prompt-injected implementer runs ln ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ./stolen && head -c 1 ./stolen in its writable worktree. If the link is created and the read is allowed, the key is read through the checkout allow.

output.summary: Reviewed the full diff (base d3e8014 to HEAD 5731023), generated the real gate and editor Seatbelt profiles from the code, and compared the affected test files against the base commit. Nested sandbox-exec is refused in this environment (`sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`), so the real-Seatbelt probes skipped (12 skipped in sandbox.test.ts) and I could not run them. Unconfined runs were not possible either. I ran scratch, gates and harness tests in a TMPDIR copy with zod 4.1.8 from the bun cache, since the worktree has no node_modules and zod 3.25 breaks config loading. Two scratch tests and the auditDiff, PR-create and cancel-preview tests fail identically on base because /tmp is not writable here, so I treat them as environmental. The change-specific regression is that 9 tests (7 scratch, 2 harness) pass on base and fail on HEAD: the editor deny list is re-resolved with strict `spellings()` on credential paths, which throws in any process that cannot stat `~/.ssh`. Switching the two call sites to the lenient mode in a throwaway copy makes all of them pass, which confirms the cause. Other findings: the gate allowlist exposes real cargo config files and home-level bunfig/tsconfig/package names, the Codex probe breaks on existing credential files, and the requested real-Seatbelt editor probes are missing. Hard-link reads were not verifiable here and are reported at low confidence.

findings.title: Strict spellings() on editor credential paths makes confined editor runs throw instead of using the lenient denied-path mode
findings.detail: `const moved = spellings(deny)` re-resolves the editor deny list with the strict resolver (policySpellings without denied=true). The same strict call exists in scratch.ts:178 (validateDenyRead, reached via readConfinement inside sandboxProbe). When a credential path such as ~/.ssh cannot be stat'd (EPERM), canonical() throws ConfinementError. read-policy.ts's `denied` flag exists for exactly this case, and homeReadPolicy/writeRoots use it, but these two call sites bypass it. Reproduced: on base, 6/6 editor-probe tests in test/scratch.test.ts and 2/2 credential tests in test/harness.test.ts pass. On HEAD they fail with 'Cannot resolve read policy path ~/.ssh' at codex.ts:812 (scratch tests: 'a leaky/timeout/admin-leak/common-leak/cancelled editor probe never starts exec', 'codex editors run only after a probe...', 'CLI sandboxes run directly when outer confinement refuses'; harness: 'a credential inside the model name never reaches the log header', 'configured credentials never reach native children...'). In a TMPDIR copy, changing codex.ts:812 and scratch.ts:178 to policySpellings(..., true) makes all 9 pass.
findings.suggestion: Use the lenient denied-path resolution at codex.ts:812 and scratch.ts:178 (validateDenyRead), or compare the already-resolved denyRead list instead of resolving it again. Add a test that runs the editor probe with a credential path made unstattable.
findings.failure_scenario: The factory's own gate runs `bun test` under the home-denying outer profile. Inside that process, realpath(~/.ssh) returns EPERM, so runCodex (edit mode) throws a ConfinementError before any verdict, and the Codex editor tests fail. The same happens to any editor launched from a confined process.

findings.title: Codex editor probe is inconclusive whenever an existing writable credential file is in the deny list
findings.detail: The negatives are built from roots(readConfinement(spec).deny), and that deny list now includes the editor credential list through validateDenyRead(spec.denyRead). canaryRoots() keeps every existing deny entry and returns a writable file as its own canary location. I confirmed this in a script: with ~/.npmrc or ~/.netrc present and writable, canaryRoots returns the file path. Then temp(root) runs mkdtempSync(join(file, prefix)), which fails with ENOTDIR. That throw is inside the try block, so sandboxProbe returns INCONCLUSIVE, and runCodex returns status 'unavailable' ('Codex write confinement not verified'). This applies to any existing writable ~/.npmrc, ~/.netrc, ~/.cargo/credentials(.toml), or a KUBECONFIG file.
findings.suggestion: Build canary roots only from directory entries of the deny list (files are checked by probeReads, which already covers them), or skip non-directory deny entries when creating canaries.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer has ~/.npmrc with a registry token, which is user-writable. Every Codex editor launch then reports 'unavailable' with an inconclusive write probe, and no Codex editor can run on that machine.

findings.title: Gate allowlist grants reads of the real cargo config.toml and config, which can hold registry tokens
findings.detail: allowRead includes join(cargo, 'config') and join(cargo, 'config.toml') for the real cargo home. Cargo honors registry tokens stored in config files (`[registries.*] token`). The generated gate profile contains `(subpath "~/.cargo/config.toml")` in its allow-read rule, so candidate code run by a gate can read it. The allowance is also unnecessary: runConfined sets CARGO_HOME to scratch and copies config and config.toml there from the factory process (sandbox.ts:249-252), so no gate needs the real file. The same applies to the cargo registry, git and bin allowances, which the scratch CARGO_HOME makes unused, but they are not credential-bearing. The GUIDE says 'Cargo registry credentials stay denied', which is not true for config tokens.
findings.suggestion: Remove config and config.toml from the gate allowRead (the trusted copy into scratch already provides them), and trim the cargo registry and git allowances to what gates actually read. Correct the GUIDE wording.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer keeps `[registries.crates-io] token = ...` in ~/.cargo/config.toml. A prompt-injected implementer's gate test runs `cat ~/.cargo/config.toml` and exfiltrates the token.

findings.title: Literal ancestor allowances expose files directly under the home directory, contrary to the request
findings.detail: ancestorReadPolicy (read-policy.ts:194) grants literal reads of package.json, bunfig.toml, tsconfig.json and jsconfig.json in every ancestor of each allowed path, including the home directory itself. The generated gate profile contains `(literal "~/bunfig.toml")`, `(literal "~/package.json")` and similar rules, so a gate can read ~/bunfig.toml. The request explicitly requires that 'a file directly under the home directory is denied'. The test (sandbox.test.ts:69 region) probes `personal`, not these names. Bun's bunfig.toml can carry `[install.scopes]` tokens.
findings.suggestion: Do not grant literal content reads for the home directory or its direct children. Keep metadata-only access for ancestors, and grant content reads only for manifest names under the allowed roots' own directories. Add a probe that reads ~/bunfig.toml and expects denial.
findings.failure_scenario: A user's ~/bunfig.toml has a registry token in [install.scopes]. A gate's test script reads it through the literal allowance and sends it out, despite the home-wide deny.

findings.title: No real-Seatbelt or real-Codex probes for the required editor credential denials
findings.detail: The request requires real probes, not profile text, showing that each listed credential store is denied for the Codex editor profile and for the Claude outer profile, and that checkout and scratch stay readable. What exists: (1) 'both editor profiles deny every credential store...' (scratch.test.ts:1476) checks parsed profile text only; (2) every Codex editor test goes through a fake sandboxProbe or fake codex runner (harness.test.ts:215, scratch.test.ts fake CODEX); (3) sandbox.test.ts:349 runs a real outer-profile read for only the relocated GH_CONFIG_DIR store, not ~/.ssh, ~/.config/limitless, ~/.codex, ~/.aws, ~/.netrc, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker, ~/.gnupg or ~/.kube, and it does not check checkout or scratch readability for editors. The real Codex sandbox probe never runs in the suite.
findings.suggestion: Add test.skipIf(seatbeltSkip !== null) real probes: for each credential store, run `head -c 1` under seatbeltProfile(writeRoots(cwd, scratch)) and under the Codex editor profile, assert denial, and assert checkout and scratch reads succeed.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that drops ~/.ssh from the editor deny list, or a Codex profile error that leaves the store readable, passes every test on the suite.

findings.title: Editor probe now writes canary directories into real credential stores
findings.detail: The edit probe used to clear denyRead (`denyRead: []`); the diff removed that, so the template now carries the credential list. canaryRoots() then returns writable credential directories (I confirmed `.ssh` and `.codex` are returned as canary locations), and the probe creates limitless-canary-* directories and canary files inside ~/.ssh, ~/.codex, ~/.config/gh, ~/.gnupg, and so on. They are removed through `owned`, but a crash or kill leaves them behind, and tools that scan these directories may react.
findings.suggestion: Keep canaries in the factory temp roots and check credential directories with read probes only, or canary a dedicated probe subdirectory that is not a real credential store.
findings.failure_scenario: The probe is killed after writing into ~/.ssh. Debris stays in the user's SSH directory, and a later ssh invocation can log warnings or behave differently.

findings.title: A readable credential store is reported as a write-confinement failure
findings.detail: In editing mode the readProbe returns WRITE_NOT_ENFORCED when a denied credential read exits 0. The reason is 'write profile not enforced' even though the failure is a read.
findings.suggestion: Use a read-specific reason (for example NOT_ENFORCED or a new READ_NOT_ENFORCED), and report it as a read confinement failure.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sees 'Codex write confinement not verified' while the actual problem is a readable ~/.config/gh, and looks in the wrong place.

findings.title: Editor deny list omits common credential stores, and the known-gap list does not name them
findings.detail: Editors deny only the ten listed stores plus configured paths and the DB. Common credential locations stay readable for editors and are not named as gaps: ~/.git-credentials, ~/.config/git/credentials, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.vault-token. The factory's data directory is also not denied for editors, so ~/.limitless/runs (other runs' checkouts and trial logs), repos and work stay readable. For gates, these fall outside the home deny only when LIMITLESS_HOME is under home, which is undocumented. The GUIDE names only Claude's login and Keychain. The launchd-managed SSH agent socket is also a non-file key path; I could not verify it from this sandbox.
findings.suggestion: Either add the omitted stores to the editor deny list, or name them as known gaps under #369 and #335. Document that the gate protection of other runs depends on LIMITLESS_HOME being under home.
findings.failure_scenario: An editor reads ~/.git-credentials through the Claude outer profile and pushes with it. The docs say that only the Claude login is readable, so the gap is not known.

findings.title: Diff is about twice the requested source budget, with machinery the request did not ask for
findings.detail: Source changes are 333 insertions and 38 deletions, against the request's ~150 changed source lines. read-policy.ts alone adds 211 lines: ancestor literal and metadata rules, a lenient canonicalizer, an environment snapshot, and toolchain-specific allowances. The literal-ancestor machinery is the source of the home-file exposure above.
findings.suggestion: Remove the ancestor literal rules (or narrow them as described above), drop the unneeded cargo allowances, and keep only the home deny, the allowlist and the credential list.
findings.failure_scenario: Maintainers review and audit about 330 lines of read-policy logic where about 150 were asked for, and the extra rules hide the home-file gap.

findings.title: Each gate command now launches one extra sandbox process per existing deny path
findings.detail: probeSeatbelt loops over roots.denyRead (home, each credential store, the cargo credential files, configDir and the DB files) and runs one sandbox-exec per existing path on every launch. A gate command on a machine with several credential stores pays several extra process spawns per command.
findings.suggestion: Probe all denied paths in one sandbox-exec invocation, or cache the result per profile string.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate with many setup and check commands pays several hundred milliseconds of probe overhead per command.

findings.title: Hard links into a writable root may bypass path-based read denials (unverified)
findings.detail: Seatbelt denies file-read* by path, but link(2) is governed by file-link, which the profile does not restrict. If macOS permits hard links to the user's own key files, `ln ~/.ssh/<key> <worktree>/k` creates an entry in an allowed root, and the candidate then reads it through the allowed path. I could not test this because nested sandbox-exec is refused here, so this is a hypothesis. The mechanism predates the diff for the SQLite file, and the diff extends the same exposure to the home directory.
findings.suggestion: Verify under real Seatbelt with ln and cp -l against a home-owned 0600 file. If it is permitted, add a `(deny file-link* ...)` rule for the credential and home subpaths.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate runs `ln ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 $TMPDIR/k && cat $TMPDIR/k`. If link is allowed, the key is read despite the home deny.

output.summary: Reviewed the preview confinement change against c79975c. The core wiring holds up: build, seed and serve go through runConfined with the preview scratch as the owned scratch, writeRoots protects the admin dir, the recorded .git-paths sidecar and the .git pointer, HOME and the LIMITLESS_* dirs point into scratch, and the served process keeps network (the profile is allow-default and only denies the factory daemon port). Fail-closed behaviour is covered by the verify/launch injection test. Two real problems remain: stop() can reject from an abort listener and crash the process under Bun, and the acceptance item about the repository UI preview builds and serving is only exercised with fakeConfinement, so the confined build and serve of this repository are never tested. I could not run the server-based tests here: the sandbox denies listen on 127.0.0.1 (EPERM) and nested sandbox-exec is not permitted, so the 21 failures in test/preview.test.ts were all sandbox EPERM, not product assertions, and the real-Seatbelt test was skipped. Biome and tsc were not run because no node_modules is installed. Probes run outside the worktree showed that runProcess teardown kills marked and orphaned descendants and resolves on close even with an unmarked descendant holding stdout, so I did not report a teardown hang.

findings.title: Abort-driven teardown can reject unhandled and crash the process
findings.detail: onAbort calls `void stop()`. stop() awaits `serving` and, in the catch at lines 115-117, rethrows ProcessTerminationError on purpose. The serve step now runs through runProcess, which rejects with ProcessTerminationError when marked-process termination cannot be confirmed. Before this change the serve child was a bare spawn and never produced that error. So an abort during a run can now produce a rejected promise that nothing handles. Bun exits the process on an unhandled rejection; I confirmed this with a minimal script (exit 1). No global unhandledRejection handler exists in src.
findings.suggestion: Do not leave the abort path's promise unhandled. Attach a handler in onAbort (for example `stop().catch(() => {})`, or record the error on the preview and surface it to the engine through the existing ProcessTerminationError / terminationBlocked path). Add a test where termination is forced to fail while the preview is aborted and assert the process survives.
findings.failure_scenario: A preview serve is running. The run is cancelled, so ctx.signal aborts and onAbort fires. Process inspection fails during termination (for example a ps or proc_pidinfo error), so serving rejects with ProcessTerminationError. stop() rethrows, and the void call produces an unhandled rejection that terminates the whole factory daemon, taking every other run with it.

findings.title: Repository UI build and serve are never exercised under confinement
findings.detail: The acceptance item 'an existing UI preview of this repository still builds and serves' is covered by 'repository preview builds the UI...' (line 491). That test calls the wrapper at line 26, which is bound to fakeConfinement: verify is a no-op and wrap is the identity, so the repo's real build:ui, seed and serve run unconfined. The only real-Seatbelt test (line 469) runs a probe script and a tiny serve.ts, not the repository's build:ui, seed or serve commands. So nothing shows that the repository's own UI preview still builds and serves once it runs under Seatbelt, with the write roots that production uses.
findings.suggestion: Add a darwin-only, LIMITLESS_CONFINED-skipped test that runs startPreview with the real seatbeltBackend (no fake scope) against a copy of the repository's [preview] config and asserts dist/index.html, the seeded database and /api/health. Keep the fake-backed variant as the portable check if you like.
findings.failure_scenario: The UI build writes into a location the confined profile does not grant (for example a cache resolved outside the checkout, scratch or HOME), or the served factory needs a read or write the gate read policy blocks. Every test still passes because fakeConfinement permits everything, and the regression reaches the factory only at verify time.

findings.title: Confinement docs still describe only gates and hidden commands
findings.detail: The architecture note says gates and implement-eval hidden commands use the Seatbelt boundary, that macOS is the only implemented backend, and that other platforms fail closed. Previews now also run confined and fail closed the same way. On Linux or any non-darwin host, every run that has a [preview] table now fails at the preview stage, where before it ran. The docs do not say so.
findings.suggestion: Add previews to the confinement paragraph in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, state the macOS-only consequence for repositories with a [preview] table, and note the new serve-process lifetime (marker-based teardown).
findings.failure_scenario: An operator on a Linux host reads the docs, sees no mention of previews, and expects the preview stage to work as before. It fails with 'Write confinement unavailable' instead.

findings.title: Existing teardown contract was inverted instead of kept or called out
findings.detail: The old test 'teardown does not wait for a detached grandchild holding stdout open' asserted that the grandchild survives stop(). The new test 'teardown stops a detached grandchild...' asserts it is dead. That changes preview teardown behaviour: marked descendants are now killed through runProcess marker scanning. It is a stricter and arguably better contract, but the change is not called out in the change summary, and the old name and comment were replaced rather than the change being explained.
findings.suggestion: Keep the new assertion, but explain the contract change in the commit or PR text, and note that descendants without the invocation marker are not covered by teardown.
findings.failure_scenario: A later reader assumes the old contract still holds, or a regression in marker scanning is hidden because the test's expectation was moved along with the implementation.

output.summary: Reviewed the preview confinement change in src/pipeline/preview.ts, src/harness/sandbox.ts and test/preview.test.ts against the request. The core design holds up on reading. build, seed and serve all go through runConfined with the checkout and the preview scratch as the only write roots, the git admin dir, .git and the .git-paths sidecar are protected, and a ConfinementError fails the preview closed. The serve step's network-bind is unaffected because the profile only denies outbound to the daemon port. Config env comes from the trusted base SHA, so the CARGO_HOME copy in runConfined is not reachable from candidate input. Running the preview test file here failed on loopback listen EPERM (sandbox local-binding is off), so no port-dependent test could be run. The only checks that ran were the non-port ones, and I could not run the real-Seatbelt test or the repo UI build. The findings below are minor and low-to-moderate confidence.

findings.title: Abort-triggered stop() can produce an unhandled promise rejection
findings.detail: stop() now awaits the serve promise and rethrows ProcessTerminationError (lines 115-117). onAbort calls `void stop()` (line 123), so when the outer signal aborts after a successful start and process termination cannot be confirmed, the stopping promise rejects with no handler. The original stop() could not reject this way, because stopTree never rejected. Bun reports the unhandled rejection and exits with code 1 when the process ends. Scratch removal is also skipped in that case, so the directory is left behind.
findings.suggestion: Have onAbort catch and log the stop() failure, e.g. `stop().catch((error) => log(...))`, while keeping the rejection for the explicit stop() callers that await it.
findings.failure_scenario: A preview is running. The run is cancelled, and process-tree inspection fails during serve teardown, so terminate() records a ProcessTerminationError. stop() rethrows it from onAbort's `void stop()`, which produces an unhandled rejection in the daemon, and the preview scratch stays on disk.

findings.title: Preview teardown semantics silently changed: process-group SIGKILL becomes marker kill with 100 ms grace
findings.detail: The old stopTree sent SIGTERM to the process group and escalated to SIGKILL after 2 s, and it reached every process in the group regardless of environment. The serve now runs through runProcess, which kills only processes carrying the LIMITLESS_INVOCATION marker, with the engine's killGraceMs of 100 ms (proc.ts:419). A serve that takes more than 100 ms to exit on SIGTERM is SIGKILLed. A descendant that scrubs its environment but stays in the process group now survives teardown. The test that pinned the old behavior (teardown does not kill the detached grandchild, asserting alive === true) was flipped to assert the opposite without the behavior change being called out in the request or the diff.
findings.suggestion: Either keep a grace period comparable to the old 2 s for preview serve (pass a per-invocation kill grace, or set killGraceMs for this scope), or state the change explicitly in the commit and test name so it is a deliberate behavior change.
findings.failure_scenario: A preview serve handles SIGTERM by flushing state for about 500 ms. It is SIGKILLed after 100 ms instead of after 2 s. Or a dev server started by a build step through a spawn with a scrubbed env keeps running after teardown and holds the preview port, where the old group kill would have reached it.

findings.title: The acceptance check that the repository UI preview builds and serves never runs under real confinement
findings.detail: The request's acceptance criterion says an existing UI preview of this repository still builds and serves. The test at line 491 uses startPreview, which is wrapped to fakeConfinement (line 26). That backend does not enforce anything, and wrap is the identity. The only real-Seatbelt test (line 470) uses a synthetic probe fixture, not the repository's build-ui.ts, seed or serve. So the real read policy (denyRead on home and private roots, the gate-mode allowRead for the bun toolchain, the solid plugin build) is never exercised against this repository's actual preview. The test name does not say that it runs unconfined.
findings.suggestion: Run the repository UI preview test through the real backend on darwin when seatbeltSkip is null, the same way the synthetic real-Seatbelt test does, or rename the fake-backed test so the gap is visible.
findings.failure_scenario: The UI build reads a toolchain path under $HOME that is neither in allowRead nor in the gate toolchain list. Under Seatbelt the build fails with 'Operation not permitted', and the fake-backed test still passes.

output.summary: Reviewed the diff against base 493c851 and ran the checks in TMPDIR copies (worktree untouched). Typecheck and biome pass. The new tests fail on base (26 failures in mcp-proxy and mcp-http) and pass on head when run individually with a 60s timeout; the acceptance test "shared holdout words leave PR code visible while holdout-only reports stay private" fails on base as required. Related suites pass except environmental failures (owner-diagnostics-cli cannot bind a port in the sandbox; a failure-injection barrier timed out under load). I found no path where holdout-only test text reaches a PR head: holdout scenarios are JSON handed to a verifier and never written into the tree, and holdout text in reports stays in the withheld section or is line-redacted. Two regressions and one scope issue need fixing: an over-broad holdout detail source in reports, a per-line privacy pass that scales badly with diff size and private-string count, and deleted-file diffs withheld even without holdout overlap. Cosmetic marker text is also off.

findings.title: Unknown or empty verifier criterion IDs are added as holdout details, withholding public report lines
findings.detail: collectVerification now calls details.add(criterion.id) for every row where rowKind(...) !== "public". rowKind returns "unknown" for any ID not in the spec (including every ID when spec is absent), and VerifySchema types id as z.string() with no constraint, so model-invented IDs are stored verbatim in lastVerify. Each such ID becomes a regex alternative matched against report lines. I verified on head: with a holdout present and lastVerify criteria [{id:"1"}], the public report line "Step 1 finished." is replaced by "[withheld: holdout result or quotation; 1 line]"; on base the same line is returned. With id "", holdoutBoundaryPattern("") matches at every non-word/non-word boundary, so on head all three report lines were withheld; on base they were returned. Holdout-ID collection was meant for holdout rows only.
findings.suggestion: Add the ID only when rowKind(criterion.id, spec ?? null, holdout) === "holdout", and skip empty IDs. Add a test where lastVerify contains an unknown ID ("1" and "") and a holdout is present, asserting that public report lines still appear.
findings.failure_scenario: A run with a holdout gets a verifier result with criterion id "1" (or an empty id, or any spec-less AC-n). Its report's public lines containing "1" (or every line, for an empty id) are replaced by holdout-withheld markers, although they quote nothing from the holdout.

findings.title: Per-line privacy filtering of every diff rebuilds and re-normalises all private strings per line
findings.detail: privatePatch calls privacy(line) for every line of the unpaged patch, and loadOutputPrivacy's closure builds [...entries, ...registeredCredentials()] and runs normalize() on each entry on every call. Cost is therefore roughly lines x private entries, on every page request. Base made one whole-text privacy call. Measured on a 50,000-line added file (1.68 MB diff): with 300 private strings head 1643 ms vs base 460 ms; with 3,000 private strings head 13292 ms vs base 728 ms.
findings.suggestion: Run privacy once on the whole patch first and return it unchanged when it is clean; use the per-line filter only when the whole-text check fails. The same fast path can be used for the report, and the per-line holdout redactor should be guarded similarly.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR touches a large generated file (lockfile or snapshot, tens of thousands of lines) while private-strings.txt has a few thousand entries. Each limitless_get_change call for that file takes around 13 s on head against under 1 s on base, which can exceed MCP client timeouts and makes paging through the diff slow.

findings.title: Deleted files are withheld wholesale, even when they contain no holdout material
findings.detail: Any file absent from the head tree now returns "[withheld: file absent from PR head; ...]" regardless of content. The request asks to withhold only holdout-only material, and nothing in it asks to hide deletions. I verified on head that a PR deleting a public text file returns only the marker; base returned the full deletion diff. The tool description says PR diff text for files in the pinned head is visible but does not mention that deletions are always withheld.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same privacy and holdout checks used for other reports to deleted files' base text, and withhold only when the text overlaps holdout-only material. If the wholesale rule is kept deliberately, say so in the tool description and in the request's acceptance notes.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR removes a public module with no holdout overlap. The reviewer sees "[withheld: file absent from PR head; 1 file, 40 lines]" and cannot review the removal, although the deleted text is not holdout-only.

findings.title: Withheld-section marker always says "1 section" and uses ungrammatical counts
findings.detail: withoutHoldoutSection always writes "1 section" even though the cut can cover several headings, and the file-diff marker produces "1 lines" (the test asserts this exact string). The request asks for the reason and count, so the count should be accurate and grammatical.
findings.suggestion: Count the headings that were cut, or drop the section count. Use singular/plural forms ("1 line" / "N lines") consistently.
findings.failure_scenario: A report with two holdout headings reports "1 section"; a one-line deletion reports "1 lines".

findings.title: Source change is about 147 lines against a budget of about 120
findings.detail: numstat for src is 87 insertions and 58 deletions in mcp-change.ts plus 1 and 1 in mcp.ts, about 147 changed lines. The added deleted-file query, safePath, and privatePatch account for most of the excess.
findings.suggestion: If the deletion rule (finding 3) is changed, the budget will move with it; otherwise leave it and note the overrun.
findings.failure_scenario: Not a runtime defect; a scope and review-budget note.

output.summary: Checked src/integrations/mcp-change.ts, mcp.ts and the two MCP test files against base 493c851. Ran the MCP proxy and HTTP suites in a copy of HEAD with dependencies installed (bun test: 78 pass, 0 fail). Ran the same new tests against base source: 26 fail, including the shared-holdout-word acceptance test, so the tests do show the change. Probe tests (in a copy, worktree untouched) found three regressions where ordinary report lines are withheld because of how the new prose and identifier harvesting works, plus a multi-line credential exposure that predates the change. Not run: real GitHub or live-service paths, and the Playwright/browser tests, which need a CDN that the sandbox blocks.

findings.title: Generic verifier evidence is harvested as a whole-prose holdout detail, withholding unrelated report lines
findings.detail: collect() now adds the entire trimmed evidence/publicSummary/citation of every non-public criterion as a holdout detail whenever that prose does not occur in publicSources. The comment above it says whole-prose matching applies only 'when they have no distinctive literals to harvest', but the code has no such check. Any short private evidence such as 'passed' therefore becomes a detail, and every report line containing that word is replaced by '[withheld: holdout result or quotation; 1 line]'. The base code does not do this.
findings.suggestion: Only add whole prose when it has no literal to harvest and is at least as distinctive as DISTINCTIVE_LENGTH, or drop prose harvesting and keep the literal-only behaviour. Make the code match the comment, and add a report test where a generic word from private evidence appears in a public Checks line.
findings.failure_scenario: A holdout criterion has lastVerify evidence 'passed'. The report contains 'Lint passed.' and, in the Checks section, 'lint passed'. Head returns '[withheld...]' for both lines. Base returns both lines unchanged (verified with a probe run on base and on HEAD).

findings.title: Unvalidated criterion id is added to holdout details; an empty id makes the boundary pattern match almost every line
findings.detail: details.add(criterion.id) runs for every non-public criterion, with no empty or short-id guard. VerifySchema and verificationText use z.string() for id, and raw modelOutput and owner-diagnostic JSON are not normalized through normalizeVerify. An empty id yields holdoutBoundaryPattern('') = (?<![\p{L}\p{N}_$])(?![\p{L}\p{N}_$]), which matches at every non-word boundary, including the end of any line that ends in punctuation. Both the pattern and the encoded() boundary test therefore withhold those lines. privateHoldoutDetails already guards against empty details with `if (detail && ...)`; this new call does not.
findings.suggestion: Skip empty or non-word ids, or add only ids that rowKind classifies as holdout and that match the H-n shape. Add a test with an empty verifier criterion id.
findings.failure_scenario: A verifier emits criteria: [{ id: '', status: 'met', evidence: 'Observed ok.' }], which is persisted in verifyResults[].modelOutput. Report lines 'Changed src/a.ts.' and 'Lint passed.' come back as '[withheld: holdout result or quotation; 1 line]'. Base returns them unchanged (verified by probe on base and HEAD).

findings.title: Multi-line registered credentials are not redacted in PR diff text
findings.detail: privatePatch filters per line and then re-checks the joined patch. Git diff lines carry a '+', '-' or ' ' prefix, so a multi-line credential such as a PEM key never matches the joined text. Per-line checks never see the full value either. The final privacy(filtered) check therefore does not catch it. The same gap exists in base (protect(patch) applied privacy to the prefixed patch), so this predates the change. But the new comment says the complete sanitized patch is checked, and the diff now returns more file text unredacted.
findings.suggestion: Strip diff prefixes before the complete-text privacy check (or run privacy on the new-side content lines with their prefixes removed and each line's prefix re-attached), so multi-line secrets match. Add a regression test with a multi-line registered credential.
findings.failure_scenario:
A registered credential is '-----BEGIN TESTKEY-----
abcdef0123456789
-----END TESTKEY-----' (from config.ts:198 or an env var holding a PEM). A PR file contains those three lines. The diff returns '+-----BEGIN TESTKEY-----
+abcdef0123456789
+-----END TESTKEY-----' unredacted. Verified with a probe on HEAD and on base.

findings.title: A holdout token match withholds the whole report line, labelled as a holdout quotation
findings.detail: holdoutRedact now replaces any line containing any holdout detail match with '[withheld: holdout result or quotation; 1 line]'. Base replaced only the matched token with '[private detail]'. A numeric or generic token that was harvested from verifier observed text, not from a quotation, therefore removes the whole line and gives a misleading reason. The change's title says to withhold only holdout material.
findings.suggestion: Keep token-level replacement for report lines, and reserve whole-line withholding for quotations (multi-line matches or quoted text). Use a reason that matches what was matched, or add a test that a report line sharing only a number or generic word stays readable.
findings.failure_scenario: Verifier evidence for a holdout criterion says 'Observed exit 7 from the runner.' The report line 'Build finished with 7 warnings in src/a.ts.' returns as '[withheld: holdout result or quotation; 1 line]'. Base returns 'Build finished with [private detail] warnings...'. Verified by probe on HEAD.

findings.title: Dead keep parameter and its branches remain in redactMultiline
findings.detail: The diff removed keep from holdoutRedact's call to redactMultiline, and patchStructure was deleted. The keep parameter, its flush branch (162-164), the keep-based line handling (169-182) and the keep-only prefix logic (182) are now unreachable. ripgrep shows no caller that passes keep.
findings.suggestion: Remove the keep parameter and its branches, and simplify the prefix return to the hidden-line marker.
findings.failure_scenario: No runtime failure. Future edits could rely on keep semantics that no longer run, and the dead branches have no test coverage.

findings.title: No test covers report lines that share a holdout token without quoting holdout text
findings.detail: The new tests check that holdout-quoting report lines are withheld and that shared words in the diff are visible. Nothing checks a report line with a shared token (number or generic word) that is not a quotation. That is why the over-withholding in the report paths above was not caught.
findings.suggestion: Add a report-level test where verifier evidence contains a number or generic word that also appears in an ordinary public Checks line, asserting that the line stays visible.
findings.failure_scenario: Changes to the detail harvesting or to line-level withholding can still withhold ordinary report lines, and the suite will still pass.

findings.title: Source diff exceeds the stated budget and includes harvesting beyond the request
findings.detail: mcp-change.ts has about 145 changed lines against an approximate budget of 120. The extra changes are the new prose and criterion-id harvesting (lines 237-259), which the request did not ask for, and it is that harvesting that causes the regressions above.
findings.suggestion: Remove the unrequested harvesting and any dead code to bring the change back within budget.
findings.failure_scenario: Not a runtime failure. The unrequested harvesting is the source of the over-withholding findings.

output.summary: Ran tsc (clean) and biome (one pre-existing warning in src/evals/policy.ts, untouched). Ran the affected suites on an extracted head snapshot in TMPDIR: land-queue, github-notifier and review-round pass (119/119); mcp-proxy, review-round, feed-producers and api-token-http gave 93 pass, 6 fail. Four of the six are 5s default-timeout failures that pass with a 120s timeout; the other two are api-token-http beforeAll failures because the sandbox forbids loopback listen (EPERM), so the CLI 401 test and the CLI end-to-end could not run. I ran the head test files against the base snapshot: the land-queue tests (fill, two-entry, review-round), all seven new change-view/consumer MCP tests and the CLI 401 test fail on base as required, but the notifier test "merged runs with permanently missing metadata" passes on base. I probed apiTokenHeaders directly with temp homes to check origin handling. Items 1 to 4 are functionally addressed; the findings are about test timing, provenance gaps, version skew, and some inaccurate message wording.

findings.title: Extra serial git spawn pushes four existing change-view tests past the 5s default timeout
findings.detail: getChange now runs one worktreeGit cat-file per commit (3 processes for a pinned read, previously 2 git calls). Measured on the same test files: base passes 'change view preserves PR text' in ~5.15s and head takes ~5.9s, failing with 'this test timed out after 5000ms'. 'change pages expose 2-line', 'change pages expose 3-line' and 'change pages reuse the catalogue' show the same pattern (base ~5.0s, head 6.8s on one run). With --timeout 120000 all four pass on head, so the failures are timing only, but the repo's default test runner now reports them red.
findings.suggestion: Batch the existence check into one process, e.g. `git cat-file --batch-check` fed the three SHAs on stdin, and parse the missing lines. Alternatively drop the separate head check where merge-base already proves it exists.
findings.failure_scenario: Run `bun test test/mcp-proxy.test.ts -t "change view preserves PR text"` on the head snapshot: '(fail) ... this test timed out after 5000ms'. The same run on the base snapshot passes at 5.15s.

findings.title: Notifier guard test passes on base and does not test the fill
findings.detail: The test 'merged runs with permanently missing metadata never spend reconciliation requests' passes on the base source (run with the head test file: '1 pass'). Base also skips merged runs without requests, so the test cannot detect the fix. It never checks that a saved MERGED snapshot fills mergedBy/mergedAt, which is the new behaviour in reconcileMergedRuns. The fill itself is covered only by the land-queue test.
findings.suggestion: Add a case where a merged run with null metadata and a saved MERGED snapshot is filled through reconcileMergedRuns, and assert the fields. That assertion fails on base.
findings.failure_scenario: Revert the fill branch in reconcileMergedRuns (github-notifier.ts ~159-168): this test still passes, because it asserts only the absence of requests.

findings.title: 'current head' can name a commit the PR does not have yet during a push
findings.detail: superseded(recorded?.sha) uses store.prHead, which beginPrPush writes with the intended commit while pushing is set (store.ts beginPrPush / observePrHead comment: 'a head recorded when a push began is only what the push intended, so agreeing with it proves nothing'). The message therefore says 'current head X' for a commit GitHub may never receive if the push fails.
findings.suggestion: When recorded.pushing is true, say the push to X is in progress instead of naming X as current, or name only the observed head.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict round begins pushing X. A limitless_get_change call with old pins returns 'PR head superseded; current head X'. The push then fails and the PR stays at the old head; the agent was told X is current.

findings.title: MCP approvals without consumer are still recorded as 'human'
findings.detail: reviewer = consumer === undefined ? (reviewer ?? 'human') : mcpRequestedBy(consumer). The MCP tool treats consumer as optional, and test/mcp-proxy.test.ts asserts 'human' for MCP calls without it. An MCP approval that omits consumer therefore still reads as a human approval in the feed, which is the symptom item 2 asks to remove. The optional field follows #479's requestedBy pattern, but that pattern leaves requestedBy empty, not a false human label.
findings.suggestion: Give MCP calls a non-human default such as `mcp` when consumer is absent, or make consumer required on the MCP review tool. Update the test expectation to match.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent calls limitless_review with verdict approve and no consumer. review_approvals.reviewer is 'human' and the feed reads 'approved by human'.

findings.title: New MCP client sends consumer to an older daemon, which rejects it
findings.detail: The HTTP review backend posts the whole input, so a consumer field goes to the daemon. The daemon's ReviewVerdictSchema (review-round.ts:25) is .strict() both before and after this change, and before the change it has no consumer key. During an upgrade where the MCP server is newer than the daemon, an approve carrying consumer gets a 400 'invalid review' and the approval is lost.
findings.suggestion: Either send consumer only when a daemon that accepts it is known, or ship the daemon first and document the order. Strictly, the schema could accept and ignore consumer for one release.
findings.failure_scenario: Newer MCP server, pre-change daemon. limitless_review({run, verdict:'approve', reviewedSha, consumer:'agent-a'}) returns an error and no approval is recorded.

findings.title: 401 names a fallback port origin as the token's binding when the record disagrees
findings.detail: When the hash does not match the origin record, or the origin file is missing, fallback() derives an origin from the client port and passes it to forOrigin, so the withheld callback reports that origin. The message then says the token is bound to it. Probe: record {origin:'http://127.0.0.1:9999', tokenHash:'00'}, LIMITLESS_URL localhost:7400, client port 7400. The callback reports 'http://127.0.0.1:7400', but the record binds to 127.0.0.1:9999.
findings.suggestion: Name the record's origin (pair.origin) when a record exists. When no binding is known, omit the 'bound origin' claim, or state the origin only as an inference.
findings.failure_scenario: After a rotation, the CLI reports the token is bound to 127.0.0.1:7400 while api-token.origin says 127.0.0.1:9999. The user is pointed at the wrong origin.

findings.title: Generic change-view message blames the arguments for backend failures
findings.detail: Any non-custom error from limitless_get_change, including the HTTP backend's 'Daemon HTTP 500: …' (mcp.ts:245) and malformed backend responses, now maps to 'Invalid change-view request or backend unavailable.' The first clause blames the caller for failures that are not argument errors. The issue asked for the specific failing part.
findings.suggestion: Map ZodError (argument validation) to 'Invalid change-view request.' and everything else to 'change view backend unavailable', and keep the custom refine message as its own case.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon returns 500 to a valid pinned read. The agent receives 'Invalid change-view request or backend unavailable.' and rechecks its arguments instead of retrying.

findings.title: CLI 401 test's 'unrelated' half removes the token, so the server-reason path is never exercised with a sent token
findings.detail: The second request deletes api-token before running, so no token is sent and the 401 comes from the missing-token branch. No test covers a 401 from a request that carried a matching token, which must keep the server's message. This test also could not run here: the sandbox blocks loopback listen (EPERM).
findings.suggestion: Keep the token file in place for the second request with an origin-matching record, and assert the server message is preserved. Run the test somewhere loopback binding is allowed.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that replaces every 401 with tokenMismatch, even when the token was sent, would still pass this test.

findings.title: Unknown-file condition has a redundant disjunct
findings.detail: In `!selected && (q.file > 0 || files.length > 0)`, if files.length > 0 and selected is undefined, then q.file >= files.length > 0, so the second disjunct never adds a case. The condition reduces to `!selected && q.file > 0`.
findings.suggestion: Simplify to `if (!selected && q.file > 0)`, or add a comment if the intent is different.
findings.failure_scenario: No failing input; the second disjunct is dead.

findings.title: HTTP review route can write 'mcp:' provenance
findings.detail: submitReview is shared by the HTTP route (server/http.ts:532) and MCP, and ReviewVerdictSchema now accepts consumer for both. A non-MCP caller with the API token can therefore record a reviewer of 'mcp:<name>'. requestedBy follows the same convention but is set only by the MCP path. This is a provenance label, not an access decision.
findings.suggestion: Only accept consumer on the MCP tool schema, and keep it out of the HTTP route's schema, or document that the label is self-asserted.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /api/runs/:id/review with consumer:'agent-a' records reviewer 'mcp:agent-a'.

output.summary: Reviewed the full source and test diff against base 21f8de5 and ran the relevant tests in a scratch copy of HEAD (the worktree is unmodified). Passing: test/github-notifier.test.ts and test/land-queue.test.ts (116 pass, 0 fail), and the MCP change-view and approval tests in test/mcp-proxy.test.ts (7 pass). Typecheck is clean and biome is clean on the 12 changed files. Against base source, 10 of the new tests fail as intended, which covers items 1–3. Not verified: test/api-token-http.test.ts could not run here because its beforeAll cannot bind a local port (EADDRINUSE in the sandbox), so the new CLI 401 test was not executed. I checked its logic by calling apiTokenHeaders directly; a standalone stub server could not be run for the same reason. Two confirmed defects: (1) after the reconcile backfill, the parent's run.merged feed item still carries mergedBy null while the run row has the filled value, because the feed trigger snapshots metadata only at the merged transition; (2) the CLI's bound-origin message names a fallback origin that the token is not bound to when the origin record's hash mismatches, contradicting the record. The remaining findings are minor or nit.

findings.title: Queue-landed parent keeps null merge metadata in its run.merged feed item even after the run row is backfilled
findings.detail: landed() sets merged:true with whatever observation exists. The merge path (line ~620) fetches the post-merge PR with .catch(() => null), so a failed or stale read (state not MERGED yet) writes merged:true with mergedBy/mergedAt null. The run.merged feed row is written by the feed_run_update SQL trigger only on the merged 0->1 transition, copying NEW.merged_by/merged_at at that moment; feed rows are never updated. Reconcile later fills runs.merged_by/merged_at from the saved poller snapshot via resolveMergedRun/updateRun, which does not re-emit or update the feed item. I confirmed this in a scratch copy: after the backfill the run row has mergedBy 'owner' while the feed item data is {mergedBy:null, mergedAt:null}. The test 'later merge observations fill queue-landed parent metadata' asserts only the feed count (feed().toHaveLength(2)), so it passes while the feed still disagrees, which is the inconsistency item 1 asked to fix.
findings.suggestion: Do not mark merged until metadata is known, or retry/refetch the post-merge read before writing merged. Alternatively, when the backfill fills a merged run, also update the existing run.merged feed row. Add an assertion on the parent's feed item data after the backfill.
findings.failure_scenario: Queue lands PR for round R (parent P). The post-merge gh pr view fails or returns OPEN, so landed writes P.merged=1 with merged_by NULL, and the feed item is written with mergedBy null. Reconcile later sets P.mergedBy='owner', but the feed still shows 'Merged ... merged' with mergedBy null, so feed and run record disagree permanently.

findings.title: CLI 401 names a 'bound origin' the token is not bound to when the origin record hash mismatches or is absent
findings.detail: fallback() computes origin = http://127.0.0.1:<port> and passes it to forOrigin, which calls withheld(origin). This happens on the tokenHash mismatch path (line 55) and the ENOENT path (line 49). In the hash-mismatch case the record names a different origin, but the message names the fallback. I confirmed with direct apiTokenHeaders calls: record {origin:'http://10.0.0.5:7400', tokenHash:<other>} with LIMITLESS_URL=http://localhost:9999 yields withheldFor ['http://127.0.0.1:7400'], so the CLI would print 'withheld because the requested origin differs from its bound origin http://127.0.0.1:7400', a binding that the record contradicts. Item 4 asks to name the origin the token is bound to, and this reports an unestablished one.
findings.suggestion: Report the bound origin only when the record's tokenHash matches (the forOrigin branch). On a hash mismatch or missing record, use a message that says the token has no recorded origin, or omit the origin. Add a test for the hash-mismatch case that asserts the origin in the message is the recorded one or absent.
findings.failure_scenario: api-token.origin records origin http://10.0.0.5:7400 with a hash for a rotated token. findings.title: MCP approvals without consumer are still recorded as reviewer 'human'
findings.detail: The reviewer is mcpRequestedBy(consumer) only when consumer is set; otherwise it falls back to 'human'. The test pins reviewer 'human' for undefined consumer (test/mcp-proxy.test.ts ~L93). That matches #479's requestedBy precedent, but item 2's stated defect is that MCP approvals show as 'human'. Any MCP approve call that omits consumer keeps the misattribution.
findings.suggestion: Decide explicitly. Either keep 'human' only for non-MCP callers (for example by having the MCP backend pass a default like mcp:unknown), or document that unlabelled MCP approvals stay 'human' as a known gap.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent calls limitless_review with verdict approve and no consumer. review_approvals.reviewer is 'human' and the feed shows the approval as human-made.

findings.title: 'superseded' refusal names the store's recorded head, not the PR head GitHub reports
findings.detail: When reviewableHead reports superseded, the reason uses recorded?.sha (the pr_heads row). That row can differ from the saved GitHub snapshot (headRefOid) that reviewableHead also compares against. During a push, recorded.sha is the intended head that GitHub does not yet have. In the 'superseded snapshot' test the saved PR head is headSha, but the message says 'current head' baseSha, and the test asserts this (test/mcp-proxy.test.ts:139-141). The message therefore can name a head that the PR does not have per the observed snapshot.
findings.suggestion: Name the observed head (snapshot.data.headRefOid) when it is a valid commit, or say explicitly that the head is the recorded one. Update the 'superseded snapshot' expectation accordingly.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saved PR head H2 but pr_heads still holds H1 (observePrHead was refused or not called). get_change returns 'PR head superseded; current head H1', while the PR is at H2. The agent restarts with H1 and gets the same refusal.

findings.title: Auto-merge path still writes merged:true without metadata

That is the same null-metadata merge transition as item 1, and it is not touched by this change. The feed row for it is written with null mergedBy/mergedAt and the later backfill cannot correct the feed.
findings.suggestion: Route this through the same post-merge metadata read, or document it as a remaining path for #476.
findings.failure_scenario: A run with merge policy 'auto' merges through the engine. The run.merged feed item has mergedBy null, as in feed 1388.

On base, merged runs are skipped, so the request count is also zero. The test guards the no-fetch property but does not exercise the filled-from-snapshot behaviour. That behaviour is covered only by the land-queue test, which does not assert feed data.

findings.title: Other clients still show the server's 'update the limitless CLI' text for an origin mismatch
findings.detail: Only main.ts api() and follow() get the tokenMismatch explanation. gate-slot.ts (apiTokenHeaders(url), then the daemon's error text), deploy-wait.ts (~L88-94), and the MCP httpBackend (mcp.ts:220) forward the server's 'update the limitless CLI' text (http.ts:194) unchanged. findings.title: Generic fallback message for all other change-view errors now asserts a cause
findings.detail: The catch-all message changed from 'Change view request failed; check arguments and local availability.' to 'Invalid change-view request or backend unavailable.' It now applies to every non-custom error, not only argument errors, and says 'backend unavailable' without evidence. The request asked to name the failing part and otherwise keep behaviour unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Keep the original generic text for unrecognised errors, or name only what is known (for example 'Invalid change-view request'). Do not add a cause the code did not establish.
findings.failure_scenario: A git or I/O exception unrelated to the arguments is reported as 'Invalid change-view request', pointing the agent at its arguments when the arguments were fine.

findings.title: consumer is accepted on the HTTP review endpoint and silently overrides reviewer
findings.detail: ReviewVerdictSchema is shared, so any HTTP review caller can supply consumer and get an 'mcp:' prefix. If both reviewer and consumer are sent, consumer wins without notice. The derived value can reach 204 characters (mcp: plus a 200-character consumer), above the 100-character reviewer limit in the same schema.

findings.title: Poller conflict triggers are not consumed after startup
findings.detail: `LandQueue.start()` processes pending triggers only once. After that, the only other consumer call is in the land-conflict error path. `saveGithubPr()` records a trigger when the poller emits `pr.conflicting`, but does not notify or invoke a consumer. Thus a conflict observed later for an open factory PR remains pending until another restart or land conflict, contrary to the requested poller trigger behavior.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for newly recorded poller triggers to be consumed while the daemon is running, such as by notifying a shared consumer or periodically draining pending triggers. Keep trigger creation and start operations durable and idempotent.

findings.title: Cached gate results are reused without checking their commit
findings.detail: `gateResults` records the SHA associated with its results, but the cache hit returns `results[purpose]` without comparing that SHA to the current worktree HEAD. On a resumed gates stage, the engine checks out the committed tree before this lookup; if HEAD has changed since the result checkpoint, the old result still feeds `compareGates` and can decide the stage for a commit it did not check.
findings.suggestion: Before returning a cached result, compare the stored SHA with the current HEAD and discard or rerun the result if they differ. Preserve a pending execution handle only when its request is still tied to the intended commit.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate execution finishes and its result is saved, then the daemon stops before the gates stage consumes it. Before resume, the worktree's committed HEAD changes. The resumed stage checks out that new commit, but `runGateExecution` returns the saved result because the stage, round, and purpose match; the stage can pass or block based on gates run against the previous commit.

findings.title: Reopened gate state is no longer redacted
findings.detail: Removing `redactGateData(this.state)` means persisted gate results from existing runs are trusted as-is after restart. Gate outputs can contain registered credentials; the pipeline later passes `ctx.state.baseline` into `implementPrompt` and may persist legacy gate data again. This bypasses the prior redaction boundary for resumed runs.
findings.suggestion: Restore redaction when loading run state, or explicitly redact every persisted gate result before it can be used, saved, or sent to a model.
findings.failure_scenario: A run created before this change has a secret-bearing gate output in `baseline` or `lastGates`. After restart, the constructor loads it unredacted; the next implement prompt can include the secret, and a subsequent save can preserve it.

findings.title: Settled handle cleanup can mask the original failure
findings.detail: The `finally` block awaits `ctx.save("gate-result")` after the execution settles. If that checkpoint save fails, it replaces the executor’s original error or successful result. This makes a storage fault during cleanup the reported gate outcome, obscuring the original result and potentially changing retry or failure handling.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the primary execution error/result when cleanup persistence fails, or handle and report the cleanup failure separately while maintaining a recoverable handle state.
findings.failure_scenario: The gate executor rejects with a meaningful gate error, then the `gate-result` save also fails; callers receive only the save error instead of the gate error.

findings.title: Verifier notes can leak holdout results
findings.detail: `collectVerification` calls `collect(verify?.notes)` without private-prose handling. That only harvests distinctive literals found in the holdout scenario; unlike non-public criteria evidence, the notes themselves are not retained for phrase matching. A report line quoting a verifier note that contains novel result wording but none of the scenario's distinctive literals therefore passes through `holdoutRedact`. This violates the requirement to withhold holdout results and verifier prose.
findings.suggestion: Treat verifier notes as private verifier prose when building the catalogue, using the same protected-prose handling applied to non-public criterion evidence, while preserving explicitly public gate citations and summaries.
findings.failure_scenario: A holdout expects a behavior described without distinctive literals, and `lastVerify.notes` says `Verifier observed the amber lantern glow.` A persisted report repeats that sentence outside the Holdout scenarios section. Since the sentence is not harvested from the scenario and notes are collected without private-prose handling, `limitless_get_change` returns the quoted result.

findings.title: Review duration still counts preparation time
findings.detail: The request says setup must be timed as preparation, not as the trial, and reports preparation time separately. For review trials this duration remains `Date.now() - trial.createdAt`, which includes setup and other preparation; the added preparationMs is not subtracted. Consequently review latency summaries overstate reviewer time by the full preparation duration.
findings.suggestion: For review trials, compute duration from the reviewer invocation interval (or subtract preparationMs from elapsed time, accounting for other preparation consistently), and add an assertion that a delayed setup increases preparationMs but not reviewer durationMs.
findings.failure_scenario: A review system runs a 30-second gate setup and the reviewer takes 5 seconds. The recorded review duration is approximately 35 seconds, so reports and latency summaries attribute setup time to the reviewer despite also recording it as preparation.

findings.title: Concurrent setup trials can race while rebuilding base gate metadata
findings.detail: The setup path calls `prepareEvalGates`, which calls `gatesAt` again after `prepareCase` has already called it. `gatesAt` uses the fixed sibling path `base-gates`, deleting and recreating it on every call. Review trials run concurrently, so one trial can remove that directory while another is populating or detecting gates from it, causing preparation to fail nondeterministically. This new second call creates an additional race for every setup-enabled review trial.
findings.suggestion: Reuse the gate configuration already computed during review preparation, or make the temporary metadata directory unique per call before adding this second gate lookup.
findings.failure_scenario: Two setup-enabled review trials for the same eval start together. Trial A enters `gatesAt` and creates `base-gates`; trial B removes that directory before A finishes writing or calling `detectGates`, so A fails with ENOENT and is recorded as a preparation error.

findings.title: Withholds the entire file instead of only matching patch lines

The added tests encode the broader behavior by expecting the whole file to be withheld, so they do not verify the stated acceptance criterion that unrelated content remains visible.

findings.title: A multiline match hides the entire file diff
findings.detail: When a multiline private string occurs anywhere in either blob, `privateFile` returns true and this branch replaces the whole patch with a one-file notice. The added tests reinforce the overbroad behavior by expecting the whole file to be withheld.
